title: Glossary
text:
Akaike information criterion (AIC): A criterion to compare models fitted to the same data, calculated as \[
\mathrm{AIC} = 2K - 2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
\] where \(\ell(\hat\theta)\) is the maximum log-likelihood of the model and \(K\) is the number of parameters that were estimated. Among models fitted to the same observations, the one with the lowest AIC is preferred, and only differences in AIC are meaningful. AIC ranks the candidate models: it does not tell us whether the best of them describes the data well.
Aleatoric probability: Probability interpreted as the relative frequency at which different values would be observed across all the possible replications of the same experiment or observation protocol. It relates to measurement error and to stochasticity and variability in ecological systems. This is the interpretation of probability used in this course.
Asymptote: A line that the graph of a function approaches. A horizontal asymptote is a finite limit of the function as \(x\to\infty\) (or \(-\infty\)). The upper asymptote \(a\) of the Michaelis–Menten function \(ax/(b+x)\) is an example.
Asymptotic efficiency: An estimator is asymptotically efficient when, in large samples, its variance is as small as the Cramér–Rao bound allows, so that no other regular estimator is more precise. Maximum likelihood estimators have this property under regularity conditions.
Asymptotically normal: An estimator is asymptotically normal when its sampling distribution approaches a Normal distribution as the sample size grows. For the mean of i.i.d. observations from a distribution with finite variance, this follows from the central limit theorem. The maximum likelihood estimator of any parameter is asymptotically normal under regularity conditions, centred on the parameter and with a variance equal to the inverse of the Fisher information.
Bandwidth: The standard deviation of the kernel used in a kernel density estimate. It plays the same role as the bin width of a histogram: a small bandwidth gives a wiggly estimate and a large bandwidth a very smooth one.
Bias: The difference between the mean of the sampling distribution of an estimator and the parameter that it estimates, \[
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta.
\] An estimator is unbiased when its bias is zero. Bias is a property of the whole sampling distribution: individual estimates of an unbiased estimator still fall above or below the parameter.
Central limit theorem: The mean of \(n\) i.i.d. observations from a distribution with finite variance has a sampling distribution that approaches a Normal distribution as \(n\) grows, regardless of the distribution of the individual observations.
Central moment: An expectation used to describe features of a distribution. The \(k\)th central moment is \(E[(X-E[X])^k]\). Variance is the central moment for \(k = 2\). Skewness and kurtosis are calculated from the central moments for \(k = 3\) and \(k = 4\).
Characteristic scale: The distance along the \(x\) axis over which a function changes by a fixed proportion. It is the value of a scale parameter that divides \(x\), or the inverse of one that multiplies \(x\). For the exponential decay \(ae^{-bx}\) it is \(1/b\), the distance over which the function falls by a factor \(e\).
Composition: The application of one function to the output of another, \(f(x)=g(h(x))\), where \(h\) is the inner function and \(g\) the outer function. It is used to give a function the range that a quantity requires, for example \(e^{a+bx}\) for a positive mean or the inverse logit of \(a+bx\) for a probability.
Concave and convex: A function is concave where its second derivative is negative, so that the graph bends downwards and the slope decreases as \(x\) increases. It is convex where the second derivative is positive, so that the graph bends upwards and the slope increases. The Michaelis–Menten function is concave for all \(x\ge0\).
Confidence interval: A range of values for a parameter, calculated from a sample with a procedure that has a known behaviour across repeated hypothetical experiments. Once an interval has been calculated, it either contains the parameter or it does not, so the confidence level is a property of the procedure and not a probability that the parameter lies in that particular interval.
Confidence level: The fraction of repeated hypothetical experiments for which a confidence interval calculated with a given procedure would contain the parameter (e.g., 95%). The actual fraction, the coverage, may differ from the intended level when the procedure relies on approximations.
Consistency: An estimator \(\hat\theta_n\) calculated from a sample of size \(n\) is consistent if it converges in probability to the parameter \(\theta\), that is, for any positive margin \(\varepsilon\), \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} P\left(\left|\hat\theta_n - \theta\right| \ge \varepsilon\right)=0.
\] It describes the probability of large errors, not the ordering of the estimates of two particular samples.
Continuous random variable: A random variable that can take any value within an interval of the real numbers (e.g., all positive numbers, or all numbers between 0 and 1). Its values cannot be listed one by one, the probability of any single value is zero, and its distribution assigns probabilities to intervals through a probability density function.
Correlation: A parameter of a joint distribution, such as the bivariate Normal distribution, that controls how strongly two random variables change together. For a bivariate Normal distribution, a correlation of zero means that the two variables are independent.
Coverage: The fraction of repeated hypothetical experiments for which the confidence interval calculated with a given procedure contains the parameter. It can be checked by simulation when the parameter that generated the samples is known.
Cramér–Rao bound: A lower limit for the variance of an unbiased estimator \(\tilde\theta\): it cannot be smaller than the inverse of the Fisher information, \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\theta) \ge 1/\mathcal{I}(\theta)\). The information in a sample therefore sets a limit to the precision with which a parameter can be estimated from it, whatever the method of estimation.
Critical point: A value of \(x\) at which the derivative of a function is zero, so that the function is flat there. It is a maximum when the slope changes from positive to negative, a minimum when it changes from negative to positive, and a saddle point when the sign of the slope does not change.
Cumulative probability function: The function \(F_X(x)=P(X \le x)\), the probability that a random variable takes a value at or below \(x\). It is calculated by adding probability masses (discrete) or by integrating the density (continuous), it is always between zero and one, and it never decreases as \(x\) increases. In R, it is implemented by the p* functions.
Data-generating process: The mechanism that produces observations in an experiment, survey or any other relevant research protocol. It includes ecological or physical processes, systematic relationships among variables, variation among units, measurement and sampling procedures, and observational error. A statistical model is a simplified representation of this process.
Density-scaled histogram: A histogram in which the height of each bar is the relative frequency of the bin divided by the width of the bin. The area of each bar equals the relative frequency and the areas of all bars add up to one, so the histogram can be compared with a probability density function.
Derivative: The slope of a function at a point, \(f'(x)=df/dx\): the change in the output per unit change in the input, measured over an interval so short that the curve is indistinguishable from a straight line. Its units are the units of the output divided by those of the input. The derivative of a log-likelihood is zero at its maximum.
Deterministic function: A function that assigns one output to each input for given values of its parameters, so that the same input always gives the same output. In a model for data it is the part that describes how the expected response changes with a predictor.
Discrete random variable: A random variable that takes values from a finite or countably infinite set, such as the counts \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\). A set is finite when it has a fixed maximum number of values (e.g., 0 to 4 surviving seeds out of four) and countably infinite when there is no pre-specified maximum but the values can still be listed (e.g., any non-negative integer).
Dispersion ratio: The ratio of the sample variance to the sample mean. For independent counts from a Poisson distribution it tends to be close to one, so a substantially larger ratio suggests overdispersion. It is an exploratory diagnostic and does not identify the cause of the extra variation.
Domain: The set of values of the input \(x\) for which a function is used. Many ecological functions are used only for \(x\ge0\) (a density, a size, a time).
Empirical cumulative distribution: The cumulative function of the empirical distribution: the fraction of observations at or below each value. It requires neither bins nor a bandwidth and, for continuous data, it increases by \(1/n\) at each observed value. In R, it is calculated with ecdf().
Empirical distribution: The distribution represented directly by observed data, by assuming each possible observation has a probability mass equal to its relative frequency in the sample. It describes the observed sample in a way that we can compute quantiles and moments, it is not a description of the data generating process.
Epistemic probability: Probability interpreted as how certain we are about each possible value when predicting an outcome, which depends on the knowledge or information that we have about the system.
Estimate: The value that an estimator returns for the sample that we actually observed. It is marked with a hat, e.g., \(\hat\lambda = 4\).
Estimator: A rule (i.e., a function) that we apply to a sample to calculate a value for a parameter. Since we treat the observations as random variables, an estimator is also a random variable: a different sample would give a different estimate.
Expectation: An operator that maps a function of a random variable to its probability-weighted average under a specified distribution. For a function \(f(X)\),

\[
E[f(X)] =
\begin{cases}
\sum_x f(x)\,P(X=x), & \text{for a discrete random variable},\\
\int f(x)f_X(x)\,dx, & \text{for a continuous random variable},
\end{cases}
\]

Fisher information: A measure of how much information a sample contains about a parameter, written \(\mathcal{I}(\theta)\). The variance of a maximum likelihood estimator approaches its inverse in large samples. From a sample we calculate the observed information, minus the second derivative of the log-likelihood at the estimate, \(\hat{\mathcal{I}} = -\ell''(\hat\theta)\). A sharply curved log-likelihood has a large information and a small variance of the estimator. With several parameters the information is a matrix: the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the estimates.
Four faces of a distribution: The four functions that every distribution has: the probability mass (or density), the cumulative probability, the quantile function and the random sampler. In R they are implemented by functions with the prefixes d, p, q and r, followed by a short name for the distribution (e.g., dbinom, pbinom, qbinom and rbinom).
Glivenko–Cantelli theorem: The empirical cumulative distribution of an i.i.d. sample converges uniformly (that is, for all values at once) to the cumulative distribution of the model as the sample size grows. It extends the law of large numbers, which applies to the relative frequency of one event at a time.
Half-life: The time \(t_{1/2}\) over which an exponential decay \(ae^{-bt}\) falls to half of its value, \(t_{1/2}=\log 2/b\), wherever we start. It is the half-maximum idea applied to a decline, and it is read on the time axis.
Half-maximum: The value of \(x\) at which a saturating function reaches half of its asymptote. For the Michaelis–Menten function \(ax/(b+x)\) it is \(b\). It is read on the horizontal axis and has the units of \(x\), unlike half of the asymptote, \(a/2\), which is a value of the response.
Hessian: The matrix of second derivatives of a function with respect to every pair of its arguments. With hessian = TRUE, optim() returns the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the estimates, on the scale of the parameters that were optimised. This is the observed information matrix, and its inverse (calculated with solve()) approximates the variances and covariances of the estimates.
Histogram: A summary of a sample of continuous measurements. The range of the measurements is divided into intervals (called bins) and the observations in each bin are counted. Dividing each count by the sample size gives the relative frequency of the bin. The width of the bins is a choice that changes how the same sample looks.
Independence: Two random variables are independent if knowledge about one of them does not change the probabilities for the other. Equivalently, their joint distribution is the product of their marginal distributions, \(P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2)=P(X_1=x_1)P(X_2=x_2)\) for discrete variables and \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\) for continuous variables. It is a modelling assumption: it is not guaranteed merely because observations were collected at different locations or times.
Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.): A set of random variables are i.i.d. when each of them follows the same distribution and the value of one does not change the probabilities for the others.
Inflection point: A value of \(x\) at which the second derivative of a function changes sign, so that the graph changes from convex to concave or the reverse. The slope is steepest (or shallowest) there. The midpoint \(c\) of the logistic function is its inflection point.
Invariance: The maximum likelihood estimate of a function of a parameter is that function of the maximum likelihood estimate, \(\widehat{g(\theta)} = g(\hat\theta)\). It allows us to fit a model on a transformed scale (e.g., the logarithm of a positive parameter) and to report the estimates on the original scale. Invariance carries over the estimate but not unbiasedness.
Joint confidence region: A region of the parameter space calculated so that, across repeated hypothetical experiments, it contains the combination of parameter values that generated the data with a given frequency. For two parameters, an approximate 95% region contains the combinations whose relative log-likelihood is above \(-3.00\) (half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom). It extends beyond the profile likelihood interval of each parameter, because capturing two parameters at once is more demanding than capturing one.
Joint distribution: The distribution of two or more random variables together. It assigns a probability to every combination of their values (the product space) or, for continuous variables, a joint probability density function \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) whose integral over a region gives the probability of that region.
Kernel density estimate: A smooth alternative to the histogram, calculated from a sample without assuming a model. A small smooth curve (the kernel, by default a Normal density) is placed on top of every observation and these curves are averaged. In R, it is calculated with density().
Kullback–Leibler divergence: A measure of how far a model distribution is from the distribution \(g\) of the data generating process. For a discrete variable, \[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta) = \sum_x g(x)\log\frac{g(x)}{P(X=x\mid\theta)}.
\] It is zero when the model assigns the right probability to every value and positive otherwise. Maximum likelihood amounts to minimising it, so the estimator of a misspecified model converges to the parameter values that bring the model closest to the data generating process.
Kurtosis: The fourth central moment divided by \(\sigma^4\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, so it has no units. It measures how thick the tails of a distribution are, i.e., how much of the distribution is spread far away from the mean. It is often reported as the excess kurtosis, which subtracts 3, the kurtosis of a Normal distribution.
Likelihood function: The joint probability (or, for continuous data, the joint density) of the observed sample, read as a function of the parameters with the data held fixed. For i.i.d. observations, \[
L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta).
\] It is not a probability distribution for the parameter: it does not add up or integrate to one over the parameter values. We use it to compare parameter values, and the value that the data support best is the maximum likelihood estimate.
Likelihood slice: The log-likelihood as a function of one parameter, with the other parameters fixed at one value, normally their estimates. A slice needs no optimisation, but it treats the other parameters as known, so it is narrower than the profile likelihood unless the estimates of the parameters do not depend on each other.
Limit: The value that a function approaches as its input approaches a given value, written \(\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)\), or as \(x\to\infty\) for the end behaviour. A limit can exist even where the function itself is not defined.
Location parameter: A parameter that shifts a function along the \(x\) axis without changing its shape, as \(c\) does when \(x\) is replaced by \(x-c\). It has the units of \(x\).
Log-likelihood: The natural logarithm of the likelihood. For i.i.d. observations it is a sum of log probabilities (or log densities), \[
\ell(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta),
\] which in R is calculated with the argument log = TRUE of the d* functions. It has its maximum at the same parameter value as the likelihood, and it avoids numbers that are too small for the computer to represent. Its value has no meaning by itself: only differences between log-likelihoods calculated from the same data are meaningful.
Marginal distribution: The distribution of one random variable in a joint distribution, regardless of the value of the others. It is recovered by adding the joint probabilities over the other variable (discrete) or by integrating the joint density over it (continuous, which gives the marginal density), e.g., \(f_Y(y)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\).
Maximum likelihood estimator (MLE): The value of a parameter for which the likelihood of the observed sample is highest, \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). The abbreviation is used for the rule and for the value that it returns for a sample. Under regularity conditions, MLEs are consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically efficient. In finite samples they are in general biased.
Mean or Expected value: The expectation of the random variable itself:

\[
\mu = E[X].
\]
It is the probability-weighted average value of a distribution, when it exists. For observed data, the sample mean is the expected value of the empirical distribution, which simplifies to the arithmetic mean:
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
\]

Mean squared error (MSE): The expected squared distance between an estimator and the parameter that it estimates. It combines bias and variance into one measure of the quality of an estimator: \[
\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]
= \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) + \operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2.
\]
Mechanistic function: A function derived from assumptions about the process that produces a pattern, so that its parameters measure something in the system, such as a rate or a handling time. See also phenomenological function.
Method of moments: A procedure to construct estimators by equating expectations of the model distribution (the mean and central moments) to the same expectations of the empirical distribution of the sample, and solving the resulting equations for the parameters.
Misspecified model: A model that does not contain the distribution of the data generating process, whatever the values of its parameters. The maximum likelihood estimator then converges to the parameter values that minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence, and standard errors and intervals calculated as if the model had generated the data are approximations.
Model: Mathematical approximation to the data generating process. It involves at least one distribution. Often one or more of the parameters in that distribution vary as a function of covariates or groups, either deterministically or stochastically (with additional distributions).
Monotonic function: A function that only increases or only decreases over its domain, so that its derivative never changes sign. Exponential decay and the Michaelis–Menten function are monotonic; the Ricker function is not.
Negative log-likelihood (NLL): Minus the log-likelihood, \(-\ell(\theta)\). The function optim() minimises by default, so we give it the NLL: the parameter value with the lowest NLL is the one with the highest likelihood.
Nested functions: A function is nested in another when it is the special case obtained by fixing one of the parameters of the other at a particular value. The Michaelis–Menten function is nested in the Hassell function, which has a third parameter \(c\), and is recovered when \(c=1\). Nested functions are the usual candidates in a comparison of models.
Nuisance parameter: A parameter that is needed to define the model but is not the one that the question is about. Which parameter is of interest and which is a nuisance depends on the question. A profile likelihood re-estimates the nuisance parameters for every value of the parameter of interest.
Observation: The value actually recorded in the real world (e.g., the number of seeds that survived in one particular quadrat). It is written with a lower-case letter, \(x\), whereas the random variable is written \(X\).
Overdispersion: Variation that is greater than the variation expected under a reference model, usually the Poisson distribution, for which the variance equals the mean. It does not identify the ecological cause: clustering, habitat differences, omitted predictors, detection variation and dependence among observations can all produce it. The opposite case, a variance lower than expected, is called underdispersion.
Parameter: A fixed, unknown quantity that defines a model distribution, such as the probability \(p\) of a Binomial distribution or the mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) of a Normal distribution. In a deterministic function, a parameter is a constant of the formula that stays fixed while the input varies, such as the asymptote of a Michaelis–Menten function.
Partial derivative: The derivative of a function of several variables or parameters with respect to one of them, taken with the others held fixed, written \(\partial f/\partial a\). The partial derivative of a function with respect to a parameter tells us how much the function moves, at a given \(x\), when that parameter changes slightly.
Phenomenological function: A function chosen because it has the shape of the pattern in the data, so that its parameters describe that shape (a height, a location, a steepness) and not a process. See also mechanistic function.
Plug-in estimate: An estimate obtained by replacing an unknown parameter in a formula by its estimate. For example, the standard error of the mean of Poisson counts, \(\sqrt{\lambda/n}\), is estimated by \(\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}\).
Population: The complete set of units, events, or possible outcomes to which a scientific question refers. In modelling, it may be a finite set of real organisms or sites, or a conceptual population described by a probability distribution. This is not always a useful concept, instead we will focus on the concept of data generating process.
Probability density function: The function \(f_X(x)\) that defines the distribution of a continuous random variable. The probability of an interval is the integral of the density over that interval, \(P(a<X\leq b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx\), so the density is never negative and its total area is one. A density is a probability per unit of \(X\): it is not the probability of a single value, it changes with the units of measurement, and it can be larger than one.
Probability distribution: A function that assigns probabilities to every possible set of values a random variable. For discrete random variables, it is derived through addition from the probability mass function. For continuous variables, it is derived through integration from the probability density function.
Probability mass function: The function \(P(X=x)\) that assigns a probability to every possible value of a discrete random variable. The probabilities of all possible values add up to one, and the probability of any set of values is obtained by adding the individual probabilities.
Profile likelihood: The maximum log-likelihood reached for each value of a parameter of interest, when the nuisance parameters are re-estimated for every value, \[
\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_1) = \max_{\theta_2}\,\ell(\theta_1,\theta_2).
\] In this course the re-estimation is done with optim(). A profile does not depend on how the nuisance parameters are written, whereas a slice does.
Profile likelihood interval: An approximate confidence interval that contains all the values of a parameter whose relative profile log-likelihood is above \(-1.92\) (half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom). It follows from Wilks’ theorem. It does not depend on the scale of the parameter and it follows the asymmetry of the likelihood, which is why it is the reference method of this book. Its endpoints are found with uniroot(). For a model with one parameter it is simply called the likelihood interval.
Pseudo-random sequence: A sequence of numbers generated by a deterministic algorithm and designed to have the mathematical properties needed for random sampling. It is what the random samplers in R produce, which makes simulations reproducible.
Quadratic approximation: The parabola that has the same value, slope and curvature as a function at a chosen point \(x_0\), \(f(x)\approx f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0)+\tfrac12 f''(x_0)(x-x_0)^2\). The Wald interval of Chapter 4 is based on the quadratic approximation of the log-likelihood at its maximum.
Quantile: A value below which a specified cumulative probability lies. For data, we calculate quantiles on the empirical distribution of the sample.
Quantile function: The inverse of the cumulative probability function: given a cumulative probability \(\alpha\) it returns the value \(q_\alpha\) at which that probability is reached. For a discrete variable, \(q_\alpha=\min\{x:F_X(x)\geq\alpha\}\); for a continuous variable, \(F_X(q_\alpha)=\alpha\). The median is the \(0.5\) quantile. In R, it is implemented by the q* functions.
Random variable: A numerical quantity that can take any value within a prescribed set (its support). It can be used to model error, variability or uncertainty. Random variables can be discrete or continuous.
Range: The set of values that the output \(y\) of a function can take. Composition with \(e^{x}\) gives a range of positive values, and with the inverse logit a range between 0 and 1.
Relative frequency: The number of times a value appears in a sample divided by the sample size. For independent observations from the same distribution, it converges in probability to the probability mass of that value as the sample size grows.
Relative log-likelihood: The difference between the log-likelihood and its maximum, \(\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)\). It is zero at the estimate and negative everywhere else, and it shows that only differences in log-likelihood are meaningful.
Reparameterisation: Writing the same function or distribution with a different set of parameters, each of which is an expression of the old ones. The curve does not change; the meaning, the units and the correlation of the parameters do. The Michaelis–Menten function and the Holling type II functional response are two parameterisations of one curve.
Sample: A collection of values that have been observed or simulated through a data generating process.
Sampling distribution: The distribution of the estimates of an estimator across repeated hypothetical experiments with the same design and sample size. It is an imaginary construct: in a real study we carry out the experiment once and never observe the sampling distribution itself, but we can approximate it with a simulation.
Saturating function: A function that increases and levels off at an upper limit (an asymptote), as the Michaelis–Menten function does.
Scale parameter: A parameter that multiplies or divides \(x\) wherever \(x\) appears in a formula. Changing it stretches or compresses the curve along the \(x\) axis without changing its shape.
Seed: The starting state of the algorithm that generates a pseudo-random sequence. If the same seed is set before the same simulation, R produces the same sequence again. In R, it is set with set.seed().
Sigmoid function: A function that increases slowly at first, then fast, then slowly again, so that its graph is S-shaped, as the logistic function does.
Simulation: The use of random sampling from a model with known parameters to generate possible samples, as a way of analysing the statistical properties of a model or of an estimation procedure.
Skewness: The third central moment divided by \(\sigma^3\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, so it has no units. A distribution that is symmetric around its mean has a skewness of zero.
Standard deviation: The square root of a variance. It describes the variation among observations, which is a different quantity from the standard error.
Standard error (SE): The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of an estimator, \[
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)}.
\] It describes the variation of an estimate across hypothetical experiments and has the same units as the estimate. A larger sample reduces the standard error, but it does not reduce the standard deviation of the observations.
Support: The set of values that a random variable can take. For continuous distributions, the support can be unconstrained (any real value), positive (any value above zero) or constrained (any value within a range).
Unimodal function: A function that rises to a single maximum and declines after it (a hump-shaped function), as the Ricker function does.
Variance: A measure of spread around the expected value, the 2nd central moment. For data, we calculate the variance of the empirical distribution of the sample. \[
\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X-E[X])^2].
\]
Variance of an estimator: The variance of its sampling distribution. For the mean of \(n\) i.i.d. observations it decreases as the sample size grows, whereas the variance of the individual observations does not change.
Wald interval: A confidence interval of the form \(\hat\theta \pm z\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)\), where \(z\) is a quantile of the standard Normal distribution (e.g., \(z \approx 1.96\) for a 95% interval). It relies on the sampling distribution of the estimator being approximately Normal, so its coverage can differ from the confidence level in small samples. With maximum likelihood it is a quadratic approximation of the log-likelihood around the estimate, with the standard error obtained from the Hessian. The interval depends on the scale on which it is calculated, so for a positive parameter it is calculated on the log scale and its endpoints are transformed back.
Wilks’ theorem: In large samples, twice the difference between the maximum log-likelihood and the profile log-likelihood at the parameter value that generated the data approximately follows a chi-squared distribution, with as many degrees of freedom as the number of parameters that are fixed. It is the basis of profile likelihood intervals and of joint confidence regions.
Zero-inflated distribution: A mixture of two processes: with probability \(p_0\) the observation is zero (e.g., a quadrat in which no seeds arrive), and otherwise it follows another distribution (e.g., a Poisson distribution), which can also produce zeros. For a Poisson distribution, \(P(X=0)=p_0+(1-p_0)e^{-\lambda}\), and \(P(X=x)=(1-p_0)e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!\) for \(x>0\). See How to make zero-inflated distributions.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
This document is reference material for the deterministic functions that are used in this book and for several others that are common in ecology. For each function it gives the formula, its properties, R code and a description of when the function is useful. Chapter 5 explains the tools with which the properties are derived (limits, derivatives and special points), so the entries apply these tools without explaining them again.
Every entry has the same parts: a summary of the function, a description of when it is useful and of where it comes from, its formula with the derivation of its landmarks, an example that is calculated by hand and verified in R, a figure and a practice exercise. The numbers in the examples are hypothetical and were chosen so that the calculations can be done by hand.
The symbols are those of Chapter 5. The input is \(x\) and the output is \(y=f(x)\). The parameters are called \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(d\): these letters are positions in a formula, and every entry says what each of them controls and which units it has. Unless an entry says otherwise, the parameters are positive and \(x\ge0\). The R functions use the same letters as the formulas, including c (R keeps functions and other objects apart, so c() still combines values). The papers cited in the entries are listed in Section 8.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
2.1 Linear
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a + b * x} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{straight line} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \text{all } y \quad (b \neq 0) \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows or decreases without bound, slope } b \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{crosses zero at } x = -a/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad d + b(x - c),\ \text{with } d = a + bc \text{ the value at } x = c
\end{aligned}
\]
The linear function describes a response that changes by the same amount for every unit of the predictor. It is a mechanistic function when a quantity accumulates or is lost at a constant rate, as the quantity is then a linear function of time. More often it is a phenomenological description over a limited range of \(x\), since any smooth function is close to a straight line over a short enough interval. In this book the linear function is mostly used inside another function: \(e^{a+bx}\) for a positive response and \(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a+bx)\) for a probability (see Range and composition).
The function is
\[
f(x)=a+bx,
\]
where \(a\) is the value of the function at \(x=0\) (the intercept) and \(b\) is its slope. Both parameters can be positive or negative. The derivative is the same at every \(x\),
\[
f'(x)=b, \qquad f''(x)=0,
\]
so the function has neither curvature nor special points. It has no asymptote either: as \(x\to\infty\) it grows without bound when \(b>0\) and decreases without bound when \(b<0\). It crosses zero at \(x=-a/b\), so for a quantity that must be positive the function can only be used on one side of that value.
The intercept \(a\) depends on where the zero of \(x\) lies, and it has no meaning when \(x=0\) is far from the values of interest (e.g., when \(x\) is a calendar year). In that case we write the function around a reference value \(c\) that we choose,
\[
f(x)=d+b(x-c), \qquad d=a+bc,
\]
where \(d\) is the value of the function at \(x=c\). This is a reparameterisation: the line is the same, and the slope \(b\) keeps its value and its meaning.

2.1.1 Example: sediment in a pond
Suppose that the layer of sediment at the bottom of a pond was 12 cm thick when monitoring started and that it grows by 0.4 cm/year. With \(x\) the time in years since the start, \(a=12\) cm and \(b=0.4\) cm/year. After 10 years the layer is
\[
f(10)=12+0.4\times10=16 \text{ cm}
\]
thick, and it reaches 20 cm when \(12+0.4x=20\), that is, after \(x=(20-12)/0.4=20\) years. Written around year 10, the same line is \(16+0.4(x-10)\). We can verify our math with R:

# Linear function: a is the value at x = 0 and b is the slope
linear = function(x, a = 0, b = 1) {
  a + b * x
}

# Thickness of the sediment after 10 years (cm)
linear(x = 10, a = 12, b = 0.4)

[1] 16

# Years until the layer is 20 cm thick
(20 - 12) / 0.4

[1] 20

# The same line written around year 10, at the start and after 25 years
16 + 0.4 * (c(0, 25) - 10)

[1] 12 22

linear(x = c(0, 25), a = 12, b = 0.4)

[1] 12 22







Linear functions with a = 12 and b = 0.4 (solid line) and with a = 20 and b = −0.5 (dashed line). The second line crosses zero at x = −a/b = 40.










ImportantPractice: sprint speed of a lizard



The sprint speed of a lizard is 1.2 m/s at a body temperature of 20 °C and 2.0 m/s at 30 °C. Find the parameters \(a\) and \(b\) of the straight line through these two points, with their units. Which speed does the line give at 5 °C, and what does that say about the range of temperatures over which it can be used?






TipSolution





The slope is the change in speed divided by the change in temperature, \(b=(2.0-1.2)/(30-20)=0.08\) m/s/°C. The intercept follows from one of the points: \(a=1.2-0.08\times20=-0.4\) m/s. At 5 °C the line gives \(-0.4+0.08\times5=0\) m/s, and below 5 °C it gives negative speeds. So \(-a/b=5\) °C is the lower end of the range over which this line can describe a speed, and the intercept \(a\) is the value of the line at 0 °C, a temperature at which it is of no use. Written around 20 °C the line is \(1.2+0.08(x-20)\).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
2.2 Quadratic
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a + b * x + c * x^2| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal when } c < 0;\ \text{U-shaped when } c > 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \leq a - b^2/(4c) \text{ when } c < 0;\quad y \geq a - b^2/(4c) \text{ when } c > 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope at } x = 0;\quad c = \text{half of the second derivative} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{decreases without bound when } c < 0,\ \text{grows without bound when } c > 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum or minimum at } x_{\max} = -b/(2c),\ \text{with value } a - b^2/(4c) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad f(x_{\max}) + c\,(x - x_{\max})^2
\end{aligned}
\]
The quadratic function, or parabola, is the simplest function with a maximum or a minimum. It is used as a phenomenological description of a response that is highest at intermediate values of the predictor (e.g., growth as a function of temperature), over a limited range of \(x\). It can also follow from geometry: a process that depends on a surface, such as the area of the skin or of the mouth, is quadratic in the length of the organism. Finally, every smooth function is close to a parabola near its maximum, which is the idea behind the Wald interval of Chapter 4.
Polynomials of a higher order (a cubic function has a term in \(x^3\), and so on) add one bend for every additional power and can follow almost any set of points. However, outside the range of the data they grow or decrease without bound, in a direction that is decided by the highest power alone, so their predictions there are unreliable.1 For that reason this supplement stops at the quadratic function.
The function is
\[
f(x)=a+bx+cx^2,
\]
where \(a\) is the value at \(x=0\), \(b\) is the slope at \(x=0\) (in units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\)) and \(c\) controls the curvature (in units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\) squared). The three parameters can be positive or negative. The first two derivatives are
\[
f'(x)=b+2cx, \qquad f''(x)=2c.
\]
The second derivative has the same sign everywhere. When \(c<0\) the function is concave for every \(x\) and its only critical point is a maximum; when \(c>0\) it is convex and the critical point is a minimum. Setting \(f'(x)=0\):
\[
x_{\max}=-\frac{b}{2c}, \qquad f(x_{\max})=a-\frac{b^2}{4c}.
\]
If we complete the square, we can write the function with these two landmarks as parameters,
\[
f(x)=f(x_{\max})+c\,(x-x_{\max})^2,
\]
which shows that the parabola is symmetric around \(x_{\max}\). It also shows that, when \(c<0\), the function crosses zero at \(x_{\max}\pm\sqrt{f(x_{\max})/(-c)}\) and is negative beyond those two values. A response that cannot be negative is therefore described by a quadratic function only between them.

2.2.1 Example: growth of a caterpillar and temperature
Suppose that the growth rate of a caterpillar (mg/day) as a function of temperature \(x\) (°C) is \(f(x)=-6+1.2x-0.03x^2\). The units of the parameters are mg/day for \(a\), mg/day/°C for \(b\) and mg/day/°C² for \(c\). The growth rate is highest at
\[
x_{\max}=-\frac{1.2}{2\times(-0.03)}=20 \text{ °C},
\qquad
f(20)=-6+1.2\times20-0.03\times20^2=6 \text{ mg/day},
\]
so the function can be written as \(6-0.03(x-20)^2\). It crosses zero at \(20\pm\sqrt{6/0.03}=20\pm14.1\), that is, at 5.9 and 34.1 °C, and it describes a growth rate only between those temperatures. We can verify our math with R:

# Quadratic function: a is the value at x = 0, b the slope there, c the curvature
quadratic = function(x, a = 0, b = 0, c = 1) {
  a + b * x + c * x^2
}

# Location and value of the maximum from the formulas
-1.2 / (2 * -0.03)

[1] 20

-6 - 1.2^2 / (4 * -0.03)

[1] 6

# The same on a fine grid of temperatures
temperature_grid = seq(0, 40, by = 0.01)
growth_values = quadratic(temperature_grid, a = -6, b = 1.2, c = -0.03)
temperature_grid[which.max(growth_values)]

[1] 20

max(growth_values)

[1] 6

# Temperatures at which the function crosses zero (up to rounding error)
zero_growth = 20 + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(6 / 0.03)
zero_growth

[1]  5.857864 34.142136

quadratic(zero_growth, a = -6, b = 1.2, c = -0.03)

[1] -8.881784e-16  0.000000e+00







Quadratic functions with a maximum at x = 20 and a value of 6 there, for c = −0.03 (solid line; a = −6, b = 1.2) and c = −0.01 (dashed line; a = 2, b = 0.4). Dashed grey lines mark the maximum and the value zero.










ImportantPractice: species richness and productivity



The number of plant species in a grassland plot as a function of its productivity \(x\) (t/ha/year) is described by \(f(x)=10+4x-0.25x^2\). At which productivity is the number of species highest, and how many species does the function give there? Calculate the slope at \(x=0\) and at \(x=12\), with units. At which productivity does the function return to its value at \(x=0\)?






TipSolution





The maximum is at \(x_{\max}=-4/(2\times(-0.25))=8\) t/ha/year, where the function gives \(10+32-16=26\) species. The derivative is \(f'(x)=4-0.5x\), so the slope is 4 species/(t/ha/year) at \(x=0\) and \(4-6=-2\) species/(t/ha/year) at \(x=12\). The parabola is symmetric around its maximum, so it returns to \(f(0)=10\) species at twice the location of the maximum, \(x=16\) t/ha/year.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
3.1 Threshold
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a, b)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{step} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y = a \text{ or } y = b \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value below the threshold (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{value from the threshold onwards (units of } y\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{threshold (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At the left end}: &\quad f(x) = a,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) = b,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{jump of size } b - a \text{ at } x = c \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{the limit of } a + \dfrac{b - a}{1 + e^{-s(x - c)}} \text{ as } s \to \infty,\ \text{for } x \neq c
\end{aligned}
\]
The threshold function describes a response that switches between two levels when the predictor crosses a critical value. It is used when an organism changes its behaviour or its state abruptly, for example the number of eggs that a parasitoid lays on a host as a function of the number of eggs that it carries (Hilborn and Mangel 1997; the original study of Rosenheim and Rosen 1991 used a logistic function), and more generally for the sharp transitions between strategies that models of optimal behaviour predict (Hilborn and Mangel 1997). The function is mechanistic when theory predicts such a switch, and otherwise it is the simplest phenomenological description of two levels. Chapter 8 uses a threshold function to show what a jump does to a likelihood.
The function is
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
a & \text{if } x<c \\
b & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(a\) and \(b\) are the two levels, which can take any value, and \(c\) is the threshold. The formula has to say to which side the value \(x=c\) belongs; here it belongs to the upper piece. There is nothing to derive with calculus. The two limits are the two levels, and the slope is zero everywhere except at \(x=c\), where the function jumps by \(b-a\) and has no derivative. This has a consequence for estimation: moving \(c\) by a small amount changes the function only if an observation lies between the old and the new threshold, so the methods that search for an optimum by following a slope fail for \(c\) (Chapter 8).
A smooth function that approaches the threshold function is the logistic function with a lower level \(a\),
\[
f(x)=a+\frac{b-a}{1+e^{-s(x-c)}},
\]
where \(s\) is the steepness. The larger \(s\) is, the shorter the range of \(x\) over which the function moves from \(a\) to \(b\), and as \(s\to\infty\) it becomes the threshold function everywhere except at the breakpoint: at \(x=c\) the logistic function equals \((a+b)/2\) for every \(s\), whereas the threshold function equals \(b\).

3.1.1 Example: foraging of bumblebees and temperature
Suppose that the workers of a bumblebee colony stay in the nest below 10 °C and make 6 foraging trips/hour from that temperature onwards. With \(x\) the air temperature, \(a=0\) trips/hour, \(b=6\) trips/hour and \(c=10\) °C. The function gives 0 trips/hour at 8 °C and 6 trips/hour at 10 °C and at 14 °C. A logistic function with a steepness \(s=5\)/°C gives, half a degree below and half a degree above the threshold,
\[
\frac{6}{1+e^{-5\times(9.5-10)}}=\frac{6}{1+e^{2.5}}\approx0.46
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{6}{1+e^{-2.5}}\approx5.54
\]
trips/hour, so it completes most of the switch within one degree. We can verify our math with R:

# Threshold function: a below the threshold c and b from the threshold onwards
threshold = function(x, a = 0, b = 1, c = 1) {
  ifelse(x < c, a, b)
}

# Foraging trips/hour at 8, 10 and 14 degrees
threshold(x = c(8, 10, 14), a = 0, b = 6, c = 10)

[1] 0 6 6

# A logistic function with lower level a, upper level b and steepness s
smooth_threshold = function(x, a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, s = 1) {
  a + (b - a) / (1 + exp(-s * (x - c)))
}

# Half a degree below and above the threshold, for a steepness of 5/°C and of 50/°C
smooth_threshold(x = c(9.5, 10.5), a = 0, b = 6, c = 10, s = 5)

[1] 0.4551491 5.5448509

smooth_threshold(x = c(9.5, 10.5), a = 0, b = 6, c = 10, s = 50)

[1] 8.332766e-11 6.000000e+00


With \(s=50\)/°C the logistic function is indistinguishable from the threshold function at these two temperatures.





Threshold function with a = 0, b = 6 and c = 10 (solid line) and logistic functions between the same two levels with a steepness s = 1 (dotted line) and s = 5 (dashed line). The dashed grey line marks the threshold.










ImportantPractice: seedling survival and soil water



The probability that a seedling survives the summer is 0.2 when the water content of the soil is below 15% and 0.9 otherwise. Write this function as a formula and as a call to ifelse(). What is the average survival probability over four plots with a water content of 10, 14, 15 and 22%? What is the slope of the function at 20%?






TipSolution





The function is \(f(x)=0.2\) if \(x<15\) and \(f(x)=0.9\) if \(x\ge15\), that is, ifelse(x < 15, 0.2, 0.9). The four plots have survival probabilities of 0.2, 0.2, 0.9 and 0.9 (the plot at exactly 15% belongs to the upper piece), so the average is \((0.2+0.2+0.9+0.9)/4=0.55\). The slope at 20% is zero: away from the threshold a change in water content has no effect on survival.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
3.2 Hockey stick
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a * x, a * c)} \quad \text{or} \quad \texttt{pmin(a * x, a * c)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating, with a sharp corner} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \quad (x \geq 0 \text{ in most uses}) \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \leq ac \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{slope below the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
c = \text{breakpoint (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) = ac,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{breakpoint at } x = c,\ \text{where the slope changes from } a \text{ to } 0 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \min(ax, d),\ \text{with } d = ac \text{ the plateau}
\end{aligned}
\]
The hockey stick function describes a response that increases in proportion to the predictor until it hits a ceiling. It has a mechanistic reading when a process runs at a constant rate per unit of \(x\) until a capacity is reached, as for filter feeders that take up food in proportion to its concentration until they reach a maximum uptake (the Holling type I functional response). It is also used for the number of recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock in fisheries (Barrowman and Myers 2000), for the density dependence of populations of lemmings, sheep and moose (Framstad et al. 1997; Grenfell et al. 1998; Post et al. 2002; Brännström and Sumpter 2005) and to locate the edges between habitats in a landscape (Toms and Lesperance 2003). Bacon and Watts (1971, 1974) studied how to estimate the transition between two straight lines from data.
The function is
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
ax & \text{if } x<c \\
ac & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(a\) is the slope of the first piece and \(c\) is the breakpoint. The two pieces meet at \(x=c\), where both give \(ac\), so the function has no jump. Its slope does: the derivative is \(a\) for \(x<c\) and 0 for \(x>c\), and it does not exist at the breakpoint. The plateau \(ac\) can be used as a parameter in the place of the breakpoint, which gives \(\min(ax,d)\) with \(d=ac\): the smaller of the straight line and the plateau, pmin() in R.
It is instructive to compare the hockey stick with the Michaelis–Menten function that has the same initial slope \(a\) and the same upper limit \(ac\), which is \(acx/(c+x)\). At \(x=c\) the hockey stick has reached its plateau, whereas the Michaelis–Menten function is at half of it: the breakpoint of the one is the half-maximum of the other. The two functions are the extremes of a family with a bend of adjustable sharpness, the non-rectangular hyperbola.

3.2.1 Example: uptake of algae by a mussel
Suppose that a mussel clears the algae from 1.5 L/hour of water, up to a concentration of 40 µg/L of carbon, beyond which its uptake stays constant. With \(x\) the concentration of algae (µg/L of carbon) and \(f(x)\) the uptake (µg/hour of carbon), \(a=1.5\) L/hour and \(c=40\) µg/L. The plateau is \(ac=1.5\times40=60\) µg/hour. The uptake is
\[
f(10)=1.5\times10=15, \qquad f(40)=60, \qquad f(100)=60
\]
µg/hour of carbon. The Michaelis–Menten function with the same initial slope and upper limit, \(60x/(40+x)\), gives 12, 30 and 42.9 µg/hour at those concentrations. We can verify our math with R:

# Hockey stick function: slope a up to the breakpoint c, then the plateau a * c
hockey_stick = function(x, a = 1, c = 1) {
  ifelse(x < c, a * x, a * c)
}

# Uptake at 10, 40 and 100 µg/L of carbon
concentrations = c(10, 40, 100)
hockey_stick(x = concentrations, a = 1.5, c = 40)

[1] 15 60 60

# The same with pmin(): the smaller of the line and the plateau
pmin(1.5 * concentrations, 60)

[1] 15 60 60

# Michaelis–Menten function with the same initial slope and upper limit
60 * concentrations / (40 + concentrations)

[1] 12.00000 30.00000 42.85714







Hockey stick function with a = 1.5 and c = 40 (solid line) and the Michaelis–Menten function with the same initial slope and upper limit (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the breakpoint and the plateau ac = 60.










ImportantPractice: recruits and spawners



The number of recruits of a fish stock increases by 3 recruits per spawner and levels off at 600 recruits. Where is the breakpoint of this hockey stick function? How many recruits does it give for 150 and for 450 spawners? Write the function with pmin().






TipSolution





The plateau is \(ac=600\) recruits and the slope is \(a=3\) recruits per spawner, so the breakpoint is at \(c=600/3=200\) spawners. For 150 spawners, below the breakpoint, the function gives \(3\times150=450\) recruits, and for 450 spawners it gives the plateau of 600 recruits. In R the function is pmin(3 * x, 600).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
3.3 Piecewise linear
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a + b * x, a + b * c + d * (x - c))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{two straight lines that meet at a corner} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \text{all } y \text{ when } b \text{ and } d \text{ have the same sign};\quad
y \leq a + bc \text{ when } b > 0 > d \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope below the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{breakpoint (units of } x\text{)};\quad
d = \text{slope above the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \quad (c > 0) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows or decreases without bound, slope } d \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{breakpoint at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a + bc,\ \text{where the slope changes from } b \text{ to } d \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a + bx + (d - b)\max(0,\, x - c)
\end{aligned}
\]
The piecewise linear function describes a response that changes at one constant rate up to a breakpoint and at another constant rate beyond it. It is the general form of the functions of this group that have no jump: the hockey stick is the case in which the first line starts at zero and the second one is flat. The function is used when an organism is expected to switch from one regime to another at some value of the predictor, for example from growing to reproducing once it has reached a certain size or age, and to locate ecological thresholds in data (Toms and Lesperance 2003). It is mechanistic when theory predicts the switch, and otherwise a phenomenological description of a relationship that bends once.
The function is
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
a+bx & \text{if } x<c \\
a+bc+d\,(x-c) & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(a\) is the value at \(x=0\), \(b\) is the slope below the breakpoint \(c\) and \(d\) is the slope above it. The parameters \(a\), \(b\) and \(d\) can be positive or negative. The second piece starts at \(a+bc\), which is the value that the first piece reaches at \(x=c\), so the two lines meet and the function has no jump. Its derivative is \(b\) for \(x<c\) and \(d\) for \(x>c\), and it does not exist at the breakpoint. When \(b\) and \(d\) have opposite signs the breakpoint is the maximum (\(b>0>d\)) or the minimum (\(b<0<d\)) of the function, and it is one that we cannot find by setting a derivative to zero.
The function can be written on a single line. The second piece is the first line plus a correction of the slope that applies only beyond the breakpoint,
\[
f(x)=a+bx+(d-b)\max(0,\,x-c),
\]
where \(\max(0,x-c)\) is zero up to the breakpoint and equal to the distance from it afterwards (pmax(0, x - c) in R). In this form \(d-b\) is the change in slope at the breakpoint, and a function with several breakpoints is obtained by adding one such term for each of them.
A piecewise linear function with many breakpoints can follow any relationship, at the cost of a corner at each breakpoint. Splines remove the corners: they are piecewise cubic functions whose pieces join smoothly at points called knots. They are used when we want a smooth curve through the data and do not need to interpret its parameters (Wood 2001, 2006), so they are not described further in this supplement.

3.3.1 Example: growth of a fish before and after maturity
Suppose that a fish is 4 cm long when it hatches, grows by 8 cm/year until it matures at an age of 3 years, and by 2 cm/year afterwards, when part of its energy goes to reproduction. With \(x\) the age in years and \(f(x)\) the length in cm, \(a=4\) cm, \(b=8\) cm/year, \(c=3\) years and \(d=2\) cm/year. The length at maturity is \(a+bc=4+8\times3=28\) cm, and
\[
f(2)=4+8\times2=20 \text{ cm}, \qquad f(6)=28+2\times(6-3)=34 \text{ cm}.
\]
The fish reaches 40 cm when \(28+2(x-3)=40\), that is, at an age of \(x=3+12/2=9\) years. The change in slope at maturity is \(d-b=-6\) cm/year. We can verify our math with R:

# Piecewise linear function: value a at x = 0, slope b up to the breakpoint c
# and slope d from the breakpoint onwards
piecewise_linear = function(x, a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, d = 0) {
  ifelse(x < c, a + b * x, a + b * c + d * (x - c))
}

# Length (cm) at 2, 3 and 6 years
ages = c(2, 3, 6)
piecewise_linear(x = ages, a = 4, b = 8, c = 3, d = 2)

[1] 20 28 34

# The same on a single line, with pmax()
4 + 8 * ages + (2 - 8) * pmax(0, ages - 3)

[1] 20 28 34

# Age at which the fish is 40 cm long, and its length at that age
3 + (40 - 28) / 2

[1] 9

piecewise_linear(x = 9, a = 4, b = 8, c = 3, d = 2)

[1] 40







Piecewise linear functions with a = 4, b = 8 and c = 3, for a slope above the breakpoint d = 2 (solid line) and d = −2 (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the breakpoint and the value a + bc = 28 that both functions have there; with d < 0 the breakpoint is the maximum.










ImportantPractice: bird species and forest cover



The number of bird species in a landscape is 5 without forest and increases by 0.2 species for every percent of forest cover up to a cover of 30%, and by 0.05 species per percent beyond that. How many species does this piecewise linear function give at a cover of 30% and of 100%? At which cover does it give 13 species? Write the function on a single line with pmax().






TipSolution





The parameters are \(a=5\) species, \(b=0.2\) species per percent, \(c=30\)% and \(d=0.05\) species per percent. At the breakpoint the function gives \(a+bc=5+0.2\times30=11\) species, and at a cover of 100% it gives \(11+0.05\times(100-30)=14.5\) species. Since 13 species is more than the value at the breakpoint, we solve \(11+0.05(x-30)=13\), which gives \(x=30+2/0.05=70\)%. The change in slope is \(d-b=-0.15\) species per percent, so in R the function is 5 + 0.2 * x - 0.15 * pmax(0, x - 30).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
4.1 Hyperbolic
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a / (b + x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{decreasing, convex} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a/b \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{numerator (units of } y \text{ times units of } x\text{)};\quad
b = \text{value of } x \text{ at which the function has halved (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/b,\ \text{slope } -a/b^2 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half of the initial value at } x = b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{y_0}{1 + x/b},\ \text{with } y_0 = a/b \text{ the value at } x = 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The hyperbolic function describes a response that declines towards zero, fast at first and then more and more slowly. It is used for the performance of an individual as a function of the density of its neighbours, for example the number of seeds that a plant produces as a function of the number of plants around it (Pacala and Silander 1987, 1990). The constant \(b\) in the denominator keeps the function finite at \(x=0\), where the simpler form \(a/x\) would be infinite. A mechanistic derivation exists when a total saturates: if the total seed production of a stand follows the Michaelis–Menten function \(ax/(b+x)\) of its density \(x\), the production per plant is that total divided by \(x\), which is \(a/(b+x)\).
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{a}{b+x},
\]
where \(b\) has the units of \(x\) and \(a\) has the units of \(y\) multiplied by those of \(x\). At \(x=0\) the function equals \(a/b\), and as \(x\to\infty\) the denominator grows without bound, so \(f(x)\to0\). For large \(x\) the function is close to \(a/x\). Writing it as \(a(b+x)^{-1}\), the power rule and the chain rule give
\[
f'(x)=-\frac{a}{(b+x)^2}, \qquad f''(x)=\frac{2a}{(b+x)^3}.
\]
The slope is negative and the second derivative positive for every \(x\ge0\), so the function decreases and is convex everywhere. Its steepest slope is the one at zero, \(-a/b^2\). The parameter \(b\) is a scale parameter (see Half-maxima and characteristic scales): if we solve \(a/(b+x)=a/(2b)\) for \(x\) we find \(x=b\), so \(b\) is the value of \(x\) at which the function has fallen to half of its initial value. In the same way it has fallen to a third at \(x=2b\) and to a quarter at \(x=3b\). Since the value at zero is easier to read from a plot than \(a\), the function is also written as \(y_0/(1+x/b)\) with \(y_0=a/b\).

4.1.1 Example: plant biomass and density
Suppose that the mean biomass of a plant (g per plant) in a pot with \(x\) plants is \(f(x)=60/(5+x)\), so that \(b=5\) plants per pot and \(a=60\) g per pot. A plant without neighbours would weigh \(f(0)=60/5=12\) g. The biomass per plant is
\[
f(5)=\frac{60}{5+5}=6 \text{ g}, \qquad f(15)=\frac{60}{5+15}=3 \text{ g},
\]
half and a quarter of that value. The slope at zero is \(-60/5^2=-2.4\) g per plant for every additional plant in the pot. The total biomass in the pot is \(x\,f(x)=60x/(5+x)\), a Michaelis–Menten function that approaches \(a=60\) g per pot, which gives \(a\) its meaning here: it is the highest biomass that a pot can hold. We can verify our math with R:

# Hyperbolic function: starts at a / b and has halved at x = b
hyperbolic = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a / (b + x)
}

# Biomass per plant (g) without neighbours, at 5 and at 15 plants per pot
hyperbolic(x = c(0, 5, 15), a = 60, b = 5)

[1] 12  6  3

# Slope at zero: D() and the formula derived on paper
hyperbolic_derivative = D(expression(a / (b + x)), "x")
eval(hyperbolic_derivative, list(a = 60, b = 5, x = 0))

[1] -2.4

-60 / 5^2

[1] -2.4

# Total biomass per pot (g) at 5, 15 and 1000 plants per pot
c(5, 15, 1000) * hyperbolic(x = c(5, 15, 1000), a = 60, b = 5)

[1] 30.00000 45.00000 59.70149







Hyperbolic functions that start at a/b = 12, with b = 5 (solid line; a = 60) and b = 15 (dashed line; a = 180). Dashed grey lines mark half of the initial value, which each function reaches at x = b.










ImportantPractice: seed production and neighbours



An isolated plant of an annual weed produces 200 seeds, and a plant with 8 neighbours per m² produces half of that. Find the parameters \(a\) and \(b\) of a hyperbolic function with these properties, with their units. At which density of neighbours does a plant produce 50 seeds?






TipSolution





The function has halved at \(x=b\), so \(b=8\) plants/m². The value at zero is \(a/b=200\) seeds, so \(a=200\times8=1600\) seeds times plants/m². For 50 seeds we solve \(1600/(8+x)=50\), which gives \(8+x=32\) and \(x=24\) plants/m². That is \(3b\), the density at which the function has fallen to a quarter of its initial value.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
4.2 Michaelis–Menten
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * x / (b + x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{half-maximum (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{\alpha x}{1 + \alpha Hx},\ \text{with } a = 1/H \text{ and } b = 1/(\alpha H)
\end{aligned}
\]
The Michaelis–Menten function describes a response that increases in proportion to the predictor when the predictor is scarce and levels off when it is abundant, because something else then limits the response. It is one of the two functions of Chapter 5, where its properties are derived step by step, and it has a different name in almost every field that uses it. In biochemistry it is the rate of a reaction catalysed by an enzyme as a function of the concentration of the substrate (Michaelis and Menten 1913), with the parameters written as \(v_{\max}\) and \(K_m\). In microbiology it is the Monod equation for the growth rate of micro-organisms on a limiting nutrient (Monod 1949). In fisheries it is the Beverton–Holt curve for the number of recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock (Beverton and Holt 1957). In ecology it is best known as the Holling type II functional response, the feeding rate of a predator as a function of the density of its prey (Holling 1959).
The function is mechanistic in each of these uses. Chapter 5 derives it for a predator that divides its time between searching for prey and handling them, and the Beverton–Holt curve follows from a mortality rate of the young fish that increases linearly with their density (Quinn and Deriso 1999). The function is also used phenomenologically for any response that rises from zero and saturates.
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x},
\]
where \(a\) is the asymptote, with the units of \(y\), and \(b\) is the half-maximum, with the units of \(x\). Chapter 5 shows that \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)\to a\) as \(x\to\infty\), and that
\[
f'(x)=\frac{ab}{(b+x)^2}, \qquad f''(x)=-\frac{2ab}{(b+x)^3},
\]
so the function increases and is concave for every \(x\ge0\), with an initial slope of \(a/b\). To find the value of \(x\) at which the function reaches a fraction \(p\) of its asymptote we solve \(f(x_p)=pa\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a\,x_p}{b+x_p} &= pa \\
x_p &= p\,(b+x_p) \\
x_p &= \frac{p}{1-p}\,b .
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(p=1/2\) this gives the half-maximum, \(x_{1/2}=b\). For \(p=0.9\) it gives \(9b\) and for \(p=0.95\) it gives \(19b\): the function approaches its asymptote slowly, and data that stop at a few times the half-maximum are still far below it.
The parameterisations in use differ in which two landmarks they take as parameters (see Reparameterisation):








Parameters
Formula
Conversion




Asymptote \(a\) and half-maximum \(b\)
\(\dfrac{ax}{b+x}\)



Attack rate \(\alpha\) and handling time \(H\) (Holling type II)
\(\dfrac{\alpha x}{1+\alpha Hx}\)
\(a=1/H\), \(b=1/(\alpha H)\)


Asymptote \(a\) and initial slope \(s\)
\(\dfrac{asx}{a+sx}\)
\(s=a/b\)



The attack rate \(\alpha\) of the second form is the initial slope \(s\) of the third one.

4.2.1 Example: growth of algae and phosphate
Suppose that the growth rate of a population of algae (1/day) as a function of the concentration of phosphate \(x\) (µmol/L) is \(f(x)=1.2x/(0.5+x)\). The asymptote is \(a=1.2\)/day and the half-maximum is \(b=0.5\) µmol/L. The growth rate is
\[
f(0.5)=\frac{1.2\times0.5}{0.5+0.5}=0.6 \text{/day},
\qquad
f(2)=\frac{1.2\times2}{0.5+2}=0.96 \text{/day},
\]
half and 80% of the asymptote (note that \(2=4b\), which is \(p/(1-p)\) times \(b\) for \(p=0.8\)). The initial slope is \(a/b=2.4\) (1/day)/(µmol/L), and the algae need \(19b=9.5\) µmol/L to grow at 95% of their maximum rate. We can verify our math with R:

# Michaelis–Menten function: asymptote a and half-maximum b
michaelis_menten = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x)
}

# Growth rate (1/day) at 0.5 and 2 µmol/L
michaelis_menten(x = c(0.5, 2), a = 1.2, b = 0.5)

[1] 0.60 0.96

# Concentrations at which the function reaches 80%, 90% and 95% of its asymptote
fractions = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95)
fractions / (1 - fractions) * 0.5

[1] 2.0 4.5 9.5

michaelis_menten(x = c(2, 4.5, 9.5), a = 1.2, b = 0.5) / 1.2

[1] 0.80 0.90 0.95

# The same function written with the attack rate and the handling time,
# and with the asymptote and the initial slope
alpha = 1.2 / 0.5
H = 1 / 1.2
alpha * c(0.5, 2) / (1 + alpha * H * c(0.5, 2))

[1] 0.60 0.96

1.2 * 2.4 * c(0.5, 2) / (1.2 + 2.4 * c(0.5, 2))

[1] 0.60 0.96







Michaelis–Menten functions with an asymptote a = 1.2 (dashed grey line) and a half-maximum b = 0.5 (solid line) and b = 2 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the two half-maxima, at which each function reaches a/2 = 0.6.










ImportantPractice: nectar intake of a bumblebee



The nectar intake of a bumblebee (µL/min) increases with the density of flowers and approaches 50 µL/min. At a density of 12 flowers/m² the intake is 40 µL/min. Find the half-maximum \(b\) of a Michaelis–Menten function with these properties. What is its initial slope, and which density of flowers gives 90% of the maximum intake?






TipSolution





An intake of 40 µL/min is a fraction \(p=0.8\) of the asymptote \(a=50\) µL/min, and that fraction is reached at \(x_p=\dfrac{p}{1-p}\,b=4b\). So \(4b=12\) and \(b=3\) flowers/m². The initial slope is \(a/b=50/3\approx16.7\) (µL/min)/(flowers/m²), and 90% of the maximum intake requires \(9b=27\) flowers/m².

title: Deterministic functions
text:
4.3 Holling type III
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{half-maximum (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = b;\ \text{inflection point at } x = b/\sqrt{3},\ \text{with value } a/4 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{\alpha x^2}{1 + \alpha Hx^2},\ \text{with } a = 1/H \text{ and } b = 1/\sqrt{\alpha H}
\end{aligned}
\]
The Holling type III function describes a response that increases slowly when the predictor is scarce, accelerates and then levels off. It is the Michaelis–Menten function with \(x\) replaced by \(x^2\) and the half-maximum by its square, which turns a saturating function into a sigmoid one. As a functional response it describes predators that kill a smaller proportion of the prey when the prey are rare, which can result from predators that switch from rare to common prey, from predators that aggregate where prey are abundant and from other forms of heterogeneity (Morris 1997). A mechanistic derivation exists: if the attack rate of the disc equation is proportional to the density of the prey, \(\alpha x\) in the place of \(\alpha\), the equation becomes \(\alpha x^2/(1+\alpha Hx^2)\).
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{ax^2}{b^2+x^2},
\]
where \(a\) is the asymptote, with the units of \(y\), and \(b\) is the half-maximum, with the units of \(x\). At \(x=0\) the function is zero. For small \(x\) the denominator is close to \(b^2\), so \(f(x)\approx(a/b^2)\,x^2\): the function starts as a parabola, with a slope of zero. Dividing the numerator and the denominator by \(x^2\) gives \(a/(b^2/x^2+1)\), which tends to \(a\) as \(x\to\infty\). The quotient rule gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{2ax\left(b^2+x^2\right)-ax^2\times2x}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^2}
=\frac{2ab^2x}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^2}, \\
f''(x) &= \frac{2ab^2\left(b^2-3x^2\right)}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The slope is positive for every \(x>0\), so the function increases. The second derivative is zero where \(b^2-3x^2=0\), positive below that value and negative above it, so the inflection point is at
\[
x=\frac{b}{\sqrt{3}}\approx0.58\,b, \qquad
f\left(\frac{b}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{a\,b^2/3}{b^2+b^2/3}=\frac{a}{4},
\]
where the slope has its largest value, \(3\sqrt{3}\,a/(8b)\approx0.65\,a/b\). Unlike the logistic function, the Holling type III function is asymmetric: it is steepest at a quarter of its asymptote.
To find where the function reaches a fraction \(p\) of its asymptote we solve \(x_p^2=p\left(b^2+x_p^2\right)\), which gives
\[
x_p=b\sqrt{\frac{p}{1-p}}.
\]
For \(p=1/2\) this is the half-maximum, \(x_{1/2}=b\), and for \(p=0.9\) it is \(3b\), against \(9b\) for the Michaelis–Menten function: the square makes the function approach its asymptote faster. In the form with the attack rate, \(H\) is the handling time and \(\alpha\) has the units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\) squared, with \(a=1/H\) and \(b=1/\sqrt{\alpha H}\).

4.3.1 Example: a bird that feeds on caterpillars
Suppose that the number of caterpillars that a bird eats per hour, as a function of the density of caterpillars \(x\) (caterpillars/m²), is \(f(x)=40x^2/(36+x^2)\). The asymptote is \(a=40\) caterpillars/hour and the half-maximum is \(b=6\) caterpillars/m². At a density of 2, 6 and 18 caterpillars/m² the bird eats
\[
f(2)=\frac{40\times4}{36+4}=4, \qquad f(6)=\frac{40\times36}{36+36}=20, \qquad
f(18)=\frac{40\times324}{36+324}=36
\]
caterpillars/hour, that is, 10%, 50% and 90% of the asymptote. A Michaelis–Menten function with the same parameters gives \(40\times2/(6+2)=10\) caterpillars/hour at the lowest of these densities, more than twice as many. The intake increases fastest at \(6/\sqrt{3}\approx3.5\) caterpillars/m², where it is \(a/4=10\) caterpillars/hour and increases by \(3\sqrt{3}\times40/(8\times6)\approx4.3\) caterpillars/hour for every additional caterpillar per m². We can verify our math with R:

# Holling type III function: asymptote a and half-maximum b
holling_3 = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)
}

# Caterpillars eaten per hour at 2, 6 and 18 caterpillars/m²
holling_3(x = c(2, 6, 18), a = 40, b = 6)

[1]  4 20 36

# Michaelis–Menten function with the same parameters at the lowest density
40 * 2 / (6 + 2)

[1] 10

# Inflection point: location, value, and slope from D() and from the formula
x_inflection = 6 / sqrt(3)
x_inflection

[1] 3.464102

holling_3(x = x_inflection, a = 40, b = 6)

[1] 10

holling_3_derivative = D(expression(a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)), "x")
eval(holling_3_derivative, list(a = 40, b = 6, x = x_inflection))

[1] 4.330127

3 * sqrt(3) * 40 / (8 * 6)

[1] 4.330127

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection point
eval(D(holling_3_derivative, "x"), list(a = 40, b = 6, x = x_inflection))

[1] -2.220446e-16







Holling type III function with an asymptote a = 40 and a half-maximum b = 6 (solid line) and the Michaelis–Menten function with the same parameters (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the asymptote, half of it and the half-maximum, which the two functions share.










ImportantPractice: a kestrel that hunts voles



The number of voles that a kestrel kills per week approaches 12 at high densities of voles, and it is 6 voles/week at a density of 20 voles/ha. Find the parameters of a Holling type III function with these properties, with their units. At which density does the kill rate increase fastest, and what is the kill rate there? Which density gives 80% of the maximum kill rate?






TipSolution





The asymptote is \(a=12\) voles/week, and half of it is reached at the half-maximum, so \(b=20\) voles/ha. The kill rate increases fastest at the inflection point, \(b/\sqrt{3}=20/1.732\approx11.5\) voles/ha, where it is \(a/4=3\) voles/week. A fraction \(p=0.8\) of the asymptote is reached at \(b\sqrt{p/(1-p)}=20\sqrt{4}=40\) voles/ha.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
4.4 Holling type IV
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid when } c \geq 0;\ \text{unimodal, with an asymptote, when } c < 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y \leq 4ab/(4b - c^2) \text{ when } c < 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b > 0 \text{ (units of } x \text{ squared)};\quad c \text{ (units of } x\text{), with } c^2 < 4b \text{ when } c < 0 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{from below when } c \geq 0 \text{ and from above when } c < 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c < 0,\ \text{maximum at } x = -2b/c \text{ with value } 4ab/(4b - c^2) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{with } c = 0,\ \text{the Holling type III function } ax^2/(b + x^2)
\end{aligned}
\]
The Holling type IV function adds a term in \(x\) to the denominator of the Holling type III function, and the sign of its parameter \(c\) decides the shape. When \(c>0\) the function is sigmoid, and it has a mechanistic derivation: it is the functional response of a predator whose attack rate is itself a Michaelis–Menten function of the density of the prey, that is, a predator that pursues prey more actively when they are abundant (Turchin 2003). When \(c<0\) the function rises above its asymptote, reaches a maximum and declines towards the asymptote. In that form it is used phenomenologically for the intake of a consumer that declines at high density, as a result of interference among predators or of defences induced in the prey (Holt 1983; Collings 1997; Wilmshurst et al. 1999; Chen 2004).
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{ax^2}{b+cx+x^2},
\]
where \(a\) is the asymptote, \(b\) is positive and has the units of \(x\) squared, and \(c\) has the units of \(x\) and can be positive or negative. Note that \(b\) is here the counterpart of \(b^2\) in the Holling type III function. The limits are found as for that function: \(f(0)=0\) with a slope of zero, since \(f(x)\approx(a/b)\,x^2\) for small \(x\), and \(f(x)\to a\) as \(x\to\infty\), since dividing by \(x^2\) gives \(a/(b/x^2+c/x+1)\). The denominator has to stay positive for every \(x\ge0\). That is always so when \(c\ge0\). When \(c<0\) the denominator is smallest at \(x=-c/2\), where it equals \(b-c^2/4\), so the function requires \(c^2<4b\).
The quotient rule gives a derivative whose numerator simplifies:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{2ax\left(b+cx+x^2\right)-ax^2\left(c+2x\right)}{\left(b+cx+x^2\right)^2} \\
&= \frac{ax\left(2b+cx\right)}{\left(b+cx+x^2\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
A quotient is zero only where its numerator is zero (see Maxima and minima), so the critical points are \(x=0\) and the solution of \(2b+cx=0\). When \(c\ge0\) the factor \(2b+cx\) is positive for every \(x\ge0\) and the function increases throughout. When \(c<0\) the slope is positive up to
\[
x_{\max}=-\frac{2b}{c}
\]
and negative beyond it, so this is a maximum. Its value follows from substituting \(x_{\max}\) in the function. The denominator is \(b-2b+4b^2/c^2=b\left(4b-c^2\right)/c^2\) and the numerator is \(4ab^2/c^2\), so
\[
f(x_{\max})=\frac{4ab}{4b-c^2},
\]
