which is larger than \(a\): the function overshoots its asymptote and returns to it from above. The closer \(c^2\) is to \(4b\), the higher the peak.

4.4.1 Example: intake of a grazer and biomass of grass
Suppose that the intake of a gazelle (g/min of grass) as a function of the biomass of grass \(x\) (g/m²) is \(f(x)=6x^2/(400-20x+x^2)\), so that \(a=6\) g/min, \(b=400\) (g/m²)² and \(c=-20\) g/m². The condition \(c^2<4b\) holds, as \(400<1600\). The intake is highest at
\[
x_{\max}=-\frac{2\times400}{-20}=40 \text{ g/m}^2,
\qquad
f(40)=\frac{4\times6\times400}{4\times400-(-20)^2}=\frac{9600}{1200}=8 \text{ g/min},
\]
and at a biomass of 200 g/m² it has fallen to \(6\times40000/(400-4000+40000)\approx6.6\) g/min, on its way down to the asymptote of 6 g/min. With \(c=20\) g/m² and the same \(a\) and \(b\), the function is sigmoid and gives \(6\times1600/(400+800+1600)\approx3.4\) g/min at 40 g/m². We can verify our math with R:

# Holling type IV function: asymptote a and parameters b and c of the denominator
holling_4 = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of biomass
biomass_grid = seq(0, 400, by = 0.01)
intake_values = holling_4(biomass_grid, a = 6, b = 400, c = -20)
biomass_grid[which.max(intake_values)]

[1] 40

max(intake_values)

[1] 8

# The values derived on paper: -2 * b / c and 4 * a * b / (4 * b - c^2)
-2 * 400 / -20

[1] 40

4 * 6 * 400 / (4 * 400 - (-20)^2)

[1] 8

# Intake at 200 and at 10000 g/m²
holling_4(x = c(200, 10000), a = 6, b = 400, c = -20)

[1] 6.593407 6.012000

# With a positive c the function is sigmoid: intake at 40 g/m²
holling_4(x = 40, a = 6, b = 400, c = 20)

[1] 3.428571







Holling type IV functions with a = 6 and b = 400, for c = −20 (solid line), c = 0 (dashed line; a Holling type III function with a half-maximum of 20) and c = 20 (dotted line). Dashed grey lines mark the asymptote and the location of the maximum of the solid curve, −2b/c = 40.










ImportantPractice: the condition on c



A Holling type IV function has \(a=5\) and \(b=9\). For \(c=-3\), find the location and the value of its maximum. Then explain what happens to the function when \(c=-6\).






TipSolution





For \(c=-3\) the condition \(c^2<4b\) holds (\(9<36\)). The maximum is at \(x_{\max}=-2b/c=-18/(-3)=6\), with value \(4ab/(4b-c^2)=180/(36-9)\approx6.67\), a third above the asymptote \(a=5\). For \(c=-6\) we have \(c^2=4b=36\), and the denominator is \(9-6x+x^2=(x-3)^2\), which is zero at \(x=3\). The function grows without bound as \(x\) approaches 3, so it cannot describe a response there. This is why the function requires \(c^2<4b\) when \(c\) is negative.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
5.1 Exponential
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * exp(-b * x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{decreasing, convex (decay)};\quad \text{increasing, convex (growth, } ae^{bx}\text{)} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } -ab \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{halves every } \log 2/b;\ \text{falls by a factor } e \text{ every } 1/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\,e^{-x/c} \text{ with } c = 1/b;\quad e^{d - bx} \text{ with } d = \log a
\end{aligned}
\]
The exponential function describes a quantity that changes by a constant proportion for every unit of the predictor. It is mechanistic whenever the rate of change of a quantity is proportional to the quantity itself: a cohort in which every individual has the same risk of dying per unit of time, litter that loses a constant fraction of its mass per day, or light that loses a constant fraction of its intensity in every layer of leaves of a canopy (Monsi and Saeki 1953). With a positive exponent, \(ae^{bx}\), it describes the growth of a population in which every individual reproduces at a constant rate.
The function is
\[
f(x)=ae^{-bx},
\]
where \(a\) is the value at \(x=0\), since \(e^{0}=1\), and \(b\) is the rate of decline. As \(x\to\infty\), \(e^{-bx}=1/e^{bx}\to0\), so \(f(x)\to0\). The rule for a constant multiple and the rule for the exponential give \(f'(x)=-ab\,e^{-bx}=-b\,f(x)\): the slope is negative for every \(x\), and at any point it is proportional to the value of the function. The second derivative, \(f''(x)=ab^2e^{-bx}\), is positive, so the function is convex.
The function has no special point, and what characterises it is a scale. An increase of \(x\) by one unit multiplies the function by \(e^{-b}\), wherever we start, so a fraction \(1-e^{-b}\) is lost per unit of \(x\). To find the distance over which the function falls to a fraction \(p\) of its value we solve \(e^{-bx}=p\):
\[
x_p=\frac{\log(1/p)}{b}.
\]
For \(p=1/2\) this is the half-life \(\log 2/b\approx0.69/b\), for \(p=1/e\) it is the characteristic scale \(1/b\), and for \(p=0.05\) it is \(\log(20)/b\approx3/b\). For exponential growth the same algebra gives the doubling time, \(\log 2/b\).
Taking logarithms gives \(\log f(x)=\log a-bx\): on a plot with a logarithmic \(y\) axis the exponential function is a straight line with slope \(-b\). In the other direction, the exponential of a straight line, \(e^{d-bx}\), is an exponential function with \(a=e^{d}\). This is the form used when the function is the mean of a count, since it is positive for any value of \(d\) and \(b\).

5.1.1 Example: light in a canopy
Suppose that the light above a crop is 1500 µmol/m²/s and that it decreases with the leaf area above the point of measurement, \(x\) (m² of leaves per m² of ground, counted from the top of the canopy), as \(f(x)=1500e^{-0.6x}\). The parameter \(a=1500\) µmol/m²/s is the light above the canopy and \(b=0.6\) per unit of leaf area is the rate of decline. Below two and below four units of leaf area the light is
\[
f(2)=1500e^{-1.2}\approx452, \qquad f(4)=1500e^{-2.4}\approx136
\]
µmol/m²/s. Every unit of leaf area intercepts a fraction \(1-e^{-0.6}\approx0.45\) of the light that reaches it. The light is halved every \(\log 2/0.6\approx1.16\) units of leaf area, and the canopy intercepts 95% of the light when \(x=\log(20)/0.6\approx5.0\). We can verify our math with R:

# Exponential decay: value a at x = 0 and rate of decline b
exponential_decay = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * exp(-b * x)
}

# Light below 2 and 4 units of leaf area
exponential_decay(x = c(2, 4), a = 1500, b = 0.6)

[1] 451.7913 136.0769

# Fraction intercepted per unit of leaf area
1 - exp(-0.6)

[1] 0.4511884

# Leaf area over which the light is halved, and leaf area that intercepts 95%
log(2) / 0.6

[1] 1.155245

log(20) / 0.6

[1] 4.992887

exponential_decay(x = log(20) / 0.6, a = 1500, b = 0.6) / 1500

[1] 0.05







Exponential functions. Left: exponential decay with a = 1500 for b = 0.6 (solid line) and b = 0.3 (dashed line); dashed grey lines mark half of the initial value and the two half-lives, log(2)/b. Right: exponential growth, a exp(bx), with a = 50 for b = 0.23 (solid line) and b = 0.12 (dashed line).










ImportantPractice: duckweed on a pond



The number of duckweed fronds on a pond grows exponentially, \(ae^{bx}\), where \(x\) is the time in days. There are 50 fronds at the start and their number doubles every 3 days. Find \(b\), with its units. By which factor does the number of fronds grow per day, and how many fronds are there after 10 days?






TipSolution





The doubling time is \(\log 2/b=3\) days, so \(b=\log 2/3\approx0.231\)/day. Every day the number of fronds is multiplied by \(e^{b}=2^{1/3}\approx1.26\), an increase of 26% per day. After 10 days there are \(50e^{0.231\times10}=50\times2^{10/3}\approx504\) fronds, which is a little more than three doublings (\(50\times2^3=400\)).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
5.2 Saturating exponential
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * (1 - exp(-b * x))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } ab \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = \log 2/b;\ \text{a fraction } 1 - 1/e \text{ of the asymptote at } x = 1/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad d + a\left(1 - e^{-bx}\right),\ \text{which starts at } d \text{ and approaches } d + a
\end{aligned}
\]
The saturating exponential function describes a response that approaches an upper limit, at a rate that is proportional to the distance that remains to that limit. This is its mechanism, and it appears under several names. It is also called the monomolecular function. In epidemiology it is the catalytic curve, the fraction of a cohort that has been infected by a given age when the risk of infection per unit of time is constant (Anderson and May 1991). It is the simplest form of the von Bertalanffy growth curve (Essington et al. 2001), and it was used by Skellam (1951) for the number of offspring as a function of the number of adults (see also Brännström and Sumpter 2005). In this book it is the response function of the practical of Chapter 6 and of Chapter 7.
The function is
\[
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right),
\]
where \(a\) is the asymptote and \(b\) is the rate at which the function approaches it. At \(x=0\) the exponential equals 1 and \(f(0)=0\); as \(x\to\infty\) the exponential tends to zero and \(f(x)\to a\). The derivatives are
\[
f'(x)=ab\,e^{-bx}, \qquad f''(x)=-ab^2e^{-bx},
\]
so the function increases, with an initial slope \(ab\), and is concave everywhere. Note that \(f'(x)=b\left(a-f(x)\right)\): the slope is proportional to the distance to the asymptote. To find where the function reaches a fraction \(p\) of its asymptote we solve \(1-e^{-bx}=p\):
\[
x_p=\frac{\log\left(1/(1-p)\right)}{b}.
\]
The half-maximum is \(x_{1/2}=\log 2/b\). At the characteristic scale \(x=1/b\) the function has reached \(1-1/e\approx63\%\) of its asymptote, and it reaches 90% at \(\log(10)/b\approx2.3/b\). A Michaelis–Menten function with the same asymptote and the same initial slope has its half-maximum at \(1/b\) and reaches 90% only at \(9/b\), so the saturating exponential bends more sharply towards its asymptote.
Two shifted and scaled forms of this function are used in later chapters (see Shifting and scaling). The first one adds a value at zero,
\[
f(x)=d+a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right),
\]
which starts at \(d\) and approaches \(d+a\); Chapters 6 and 7 write it as \(r+a\left(1-e^{-kx}\right)\) for the response of photosynthesis to light. The second one takes the value at zero, \(y_0\), and the asymptote, \(y_\infty\), as parameters,
\[
f(x)=y_\infty-\left(y_\infty-y_0\right)e^{-bx},
\]
and it is the same function with \(d=y_0\) and \(a=y_\infty-y_0\); the practical of Chapter 7 writes it as \(A-(A-R_0)e^{-kt}\) for the growth of trees.

5.2.1 Example: infection and age
Suppose that the animals of a population are exposed to a parasite at a constant rate of 0.4 infections per animal per year from birth, and that an infected animal remains recognisable as such. The fraction of animals of age \(x\) (years) that has been infected is then \(f(x)=1-e^{-0.4x}\), a saturating exponential with \(a=1\) (a fraction, without units) and \(b=0.4\)/year. At an age of 1 and of 5 years:
\[
f(1)=1-e^{-0.4}\approx0.33, \qquad f(5)=1-e^{-2}\approx0.86.
\]
Half of the animals have been infected at an age of \(\log 2/0.4\approx1.7\) years and 90% at \(\log(10)/0.4\approx5.8\) years. The initial slope is \(ab=0.4\)/year, the rate of infection itself.
For the shifted form, suppose that the net photosynthesis of a leaf (µmol/m²/s) as a function of light \(x\) (µmol/m²/s) is \(f(x)=-1.5+16.5\left(1-e^{-0.004x}\right)\). It starts at \(d=-1.5\) in the dark and approaches \(d+a=15\). At \(x=500\) it is \(-1.5+16.5\left(1-e^{-2}\right)\approx12.8\), and it is zero at the light intensity that solves \(16.5\left(1-e^{-0.004x}\right)=1.5\), that is, at \(x=\log\left(1/(1-1.5/16.5)\right)/0.004\approx23.8\) µmol/m²/s. We can verify our math with R:

# Saturating exponential: asymptote a and rate b
saturating_exponential = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * (1 - exp(-b * x))
}

# Fraction infected at 1 and 5 years
saturating_exponential(x = c(1, 5), a = 1, b = 0.4)

# Ages at which 50% and 90% of the animals have been infected
log(2) / 0.4

[1] 1.732868

log(10) / 0.4

[1] 5.756463

# Shifted form for photosynthesis: value in the dark, at x = 500 and where it is
# zero (up to rounding error)
light_values = c(0, 500, log(1 / (1 - 1.5 / 16.5)) / 0.004)
light_values

-1.5 + saturating_exponential(x = light_values, a = 16.5, b = 0.004)

ImportantPractice: emergence of seedlings



The cumulative number of seedlings that have emerged in a plot approaches 120 seedlings/m², and 60 seedlings/m² have emerged after 7 days. Find the rate \(b\) of a saturating exponential function with these properties. After how many days have 90% of the seedlings emerged? What is the rate of emergence at the start?






TipSolution





Half of the asymptote is reached after 7 days, so \(\log 2/b=7\) and \(b=\log 2/7\approx0.099\)/day. The function reaches 90% of its asymptote at \(\log(10)/b\approx23.3\) days. The initial slope is \(ab=120\times0.099\approx11.9\) seedlings/m²/day.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
5.3 Ricker
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * x * exp(-b * x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y \leq a/(be) \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{initial slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = 1/b \text{ with value } a/(be);\ \text{inflection point at } x = 2/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\,x\,e^{-x/c} \text{ with } c = 1/b;\quad x\,e^{r(1 - x/K)} \text{ with } a = e^{r},\ b = r/K
\end{aligned}
\]
The Ricker function describes a response that increases in proportion to the predictor when the predictor is small, reaches a maximum and declines towards zero. Ricker (1954) proposed it for the number of recruits of a fish stock as a function of the number of spawners. Its mechanism is a production per individual that declines exponentially with density, \(ae^{-bx}\), so that the total production of \(x\) individuals is \(axe^{-bx}\). In fisheries the decline is attributed to competition among the young fish, for example through cannibalism (Quinn and Deriso 1999), and the same form describes populations in which fecundity falls with density (Hassell 1975; Royama 1992; Brännström and Sumpter 2005). The function is also used phenomenologically for any response that starts at zero, peaks and falls. It is one of the two functions of Chapter 5, where its properties are derived.
The function is
\[
f(x)=axe^{-bx},
\]
where \(a\) is the initial slope and \(b\) is the rate at which the production per individual declines. Chapter 5 shows that
\[
f'(x)=a(1-bx)\,e^{-bx}, \qquad f''(x)=-ab(2-bx)\,e^{-bx},
\]
which gives a maximum at \(x_{\max}=1/b\), with value \(a/(be)\), and an inflection point at \(x=2/b\), where the value is \(2a/(be^2)\) and the decline is steepest. At the maximum the production per individual is \(ae^{-1}\), that is, 37% of what it is at low density.
In population ecology the function is written with a growth rate \(r\) and a carrying capacity \(K\),
\[
f(x)=x\,e^{r(1-x/K)},
\]
which is the form above with \(a=e^{r}\) and \(b=r/K\). In this form \(f(K)=K\): at the carrying capacity the output equals the input. With the location of the peak as a parameter the function is \(axe^{-x/c}\), and the generalised Ricker function takes both the location and the height of the peak as parameters.

5.3.1 Example: seed production of an annual grass
Suppose that the number of seeds produced per m² by an annual grass, as a function of the density of plants \(x\) (plants/m²), is \(f(x)=120xe^{-0.004x}\). The parameter \(a=120\) seeds per plant is the seed production of a plant without neighbours and \(b=0.004\) m² per plant is the rate at which the production per plant declines with density. The seed production per m² is highest at
\[
x_{\max}=\frac{1}{0.004}=250 \text{ plants/m}^2,
\qquad
f(250)=\frac{120}{0.004\,e}\approx11036 \text{ seeds/m}^2,
\]
where each plant produces \(120e^{-1}\approx44\) seeds. The inflection point is at \(2/0.004=500\) plants/m², where the function gives \(2\times120/(0.004e^2)\approx8120\) seeds/m². We can verify our math with R:

# Ricker function: initial slope a and rate b
ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x * exp(-b * x)
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of densities
density_grid = seq(0, 2000, by = 0.01)
seed_values = ricker(density_grid, a = 120, b = 0.004)
density_grid[which.max(seed_values)]

[1] 250

max(seed_values)

[1] 11036.38

# The values derived on paper: 1 / b and a / (b * e)
1 / 0.004

[1] 250

120 / (0.004 * exp(1))

[1] 11036.38

# Value at the inflection point and second derivative there
ricker(x = 500, a = 120, b = 0.004)

[1] 8120.117

ricker_second = D(D(expression(a * x * exp(-b * x)), "x"), "x")
eval(ricker_second, list(a = 120, b = 0.004, x = 500))

[1] 0







Ricker functions with an initial slope a = 120 and a rate b = 0.004 (solid line) and b = 0.008 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the locations of the two maxima, 1/b.










ImportantPractice: a Ricker function in its population form



A paper describes the number of voles in a meadow in one year as a function of their number \(x\) in the previous year with \(f(x)=xe^{r(1-x/K)}\), where \(r=1.5\) and \(K=800\) voles. Write the function as \(axe^{-bx}\). At which number of voles is the function highest, and which value does it have there?






TipSolution





Since \(e^{r(1-x/K)}=e^{r}e^{-(r/K)x}\), we have \(a=e^{1.5}\approx4.48\) voles per vole and \(b=r/K=1.5/800=0.001875\) per vole. The maximum is at \(x_{\max}=1/b=K/r\approx533\) voles, where the function equals \(a/(be)=(K/r)\,e^{r-1}=533\times e^{0.5}\approx879\) voles.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
5.4 Logistic
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a / (1 + exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, symmetric around its midpoint} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{steepness (inverse units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{midpoint (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/(1 + e^{bc}) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a/2 \text{ and slope } ab/4 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}} \text{ with } a = 1,\ b = \beta_1,\ c = -\beta_0/\beta_1;\quad
\dfrac{K}{1 + \frac{K - n_0}{n_0}e^{-rx}}
\end{aligned}
\]
The logistic function describes a response that increases from a lower to an upper limit, slowly at first, fastest half-way and slowly again. In population ecology it is the size of a population whose growth rate per individual declines linearly with its density, which is its mechanism (see Adler 2004). With an upper asymptote of 1 it is the usual function for a probability that changes with a predictor, and in that role it is phenomenological: it is chosen because it stays between 0 and 1. Verhulst (1838) proposed the curve as a model for the growth of a population and later gave it its name (courbe logistique).
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{a}{1+e^{-b(x-c)}},
\]
where \(a\) is the upper asymptote, \(b\) is the steepness and \(c\) is the midpoint. The function is defined for negative values of \(x\) as well, so it has two ends. As \(x\to\infty\), \(e^{-b(x-c)}\to0\) and \(f(x)\to a\). As \(x\to-\infty\) the exponential grows without bound and \(f(x)\to0\). So the function has two asymptotes, 0 and \(a\). At \(x=0\) its value is \(a/(1+e^{bc})\), which is small when \(bc\) is large but is never zero.
For the derivative we write \(f(x)=a\,u^{-1}\) with \(u=1+e^{-b(x-c)}\) and apply the chain rule:
\[
f'(x)=\frac{ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}}{\left(1+e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^2}=b\,f(x)\left(1-\frac{f(x)}{a}\right),
\]
where the last equality follows from \(f(x)/a=1/u\) and \(1-f(x)/a=e^{-b(x-c)}/u\). It writes the slope in terms of the function itself, which is convenient: the slope is close to zero where \(f(x)\) is close to 0 or to \(a\), and it is largest in between. If we differentiate \(f'(x)=bf(x)-(b/a)f(x)^2\) once more with the chain rule, we obtain
\[
f''(x)=b\,f'(x)-\frac{2b}{a}\,f(x)\,f'(x)=b\,f'(x)\left(1-\frac{2f(x)}{a}\right).
\]
Since \(f'(x)\) is positive everywhere, the second derivative is zero only where \(f(x)=a/2\), which happens at \(x=c\) (there the exponential equals \(e^{0}=1\)). The function is convex before that point and concave after it. So the midpoint \(c\) is the inflection point of the function: the value of \(x\) at which the function reaches half of its asymptote and at which it is steepest. The slope at the midpoint is \(f'(c)=b\,(a/2)(1-1/2)=ab/4\), so for a given asymptote the parameter \(b\) sets the maximum slope. The function is symmetric around its midpoint: \(f(c+s)+f(c-s)=a\) for any distance \(s\).
To find where the function reaches a fraction \(p\) of its asymptote we solve \(f(x_p)=pa\), which gives \(e^{-b(x_p-c)}=(1-p)/p\) and
\[
x_p=c+\frac{1}{b}\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=c+\frac{\operatorname{logit}p}{b}.
\]
So the function reaches 90% of its asymptote at \(c+\log(9)/b\approx c+2.2/b\) and 10% at \(c-2.2/b\). The distance between these two points, \(4.4/b\), is a convenient way of reading \(b\) from a plot.
The logistic function has three forms that are in common use (see Reparameterisation). The one of this entry has the upper asymptote, the steepness and the midpoint as parameters. Statistical texts write the function with an asymptote of 1 as the inverse logit of a straight line,
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta_1x)}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}}{1+e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}},
\]
where \(\beta_0\) is the intercept and \(\beta_1\) the slope of the line. Comparing the exponents, \(\beta_1=b\) and \(\beta_0=-bc\), so the midpoint is \(c=-\beta_0/\beta_1\). In R this form is plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x). In population ecology, with time as the input, the function is written as
\[
f(x)=\frac{K}{1+\dfrac{K-n_0}{n_0}\,e^{-rx}},
\]
where \(K\) is the carrying capacity, \(n_0\) is the size of the population at \(x=0\) and \(r\) is its growth rate per individual at low density. In this form the function is the solution of a differential equation for the growth of a population, \(dn/dt=rn(1-n/K)\), which is where the parameters \(r\) and \(K\) come from (this book does not work with dynamical models, so we use the function only as a curve). It is the form of this entry with \(a=K\), \(b=r\) and \(c=\log\left((K-n_0)/n_0\right)/r\). Some texts write the function with the hyperbolic tangent, \(\tfrac{a}{2}\left[1+\tanh\left(b(x-c)/2\right)\right]\), which is again the same curve. A lower asymptote other than zero is obtained by adding a parameter, \(d+a/(1+e^{-b(x-c)})\), as in the threshold entry.

5.4.1 Example: maturity and body length
Suppose that the probability that a female fish is mature, as a function of her body length \(x\) (cm), is a logistic function with \(a=1\), \(b=0.25\)/cm and \(c=60\) cm. Half of the females of 60 cm are mature, and around that length the probability increases by \(ab/4=0.0625\)/cm. At 50 cm the probability is
\[
f(50)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-0.25\times(50-60)}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{2.5}}\approx0.076,
\]
and 90% of the females are mature at a length of \(60+\log(9)/0.25\approx68.8\) cm. In the statistical form the function is \(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(-15+0.25x)\), since \(\beta_0=-bc=-15\). We can verify our math with R:

# Logistic function: upper asymptote a, steepness b and midpoint c
logistic = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a / (1 + exp(-b * (x - c)))
}

# Probability of being mature at 50 and 60 cm
logistic(x = c(50, 60), a = 1, b = 0.25, c = 60)

[1] 0.07585818 0.50000000

# The same with plogis() and with the hyperbolic tangent
plogis(-15 + 0.25 * c(50, 60))

[1] 0.07585818 0.50000000

0.5 * (1 + tanh(0.25 * (c(50, 60) - 60) / 2))

ImportantPractice: height growth of a tree



The height of a tree approaches 30 m. The tree is 15 m tall at an age of 25 years, which is also when it grows fastest, at 0.9 m/year. Find the parameters \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) of a logistic function with these properties, with their units. At which age is the tree 27 m tall?






TipSolution





The asymptote is \(a=30\) m. Half of it is reached at the midpoint, so \(c=25\) years, which is also where the slope is largest. That slope is \(ab/4=0.9\) m/year, so \(b=4\times0.9/30=0.12\)/year. A height of 27 m is 90% of the asymptote, which the function reaches at \(c+\log(9)/b=25+2.197/0.12\approx43.3\) years.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
5.5 Gompertz
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, asymmetric} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{inflection point (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a\exp\left(-e^{bc}\right) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a/e \text{ and slope } ab/e \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\exp\left(-d\,e^{-bx}\right) \text{ with } d = e^{bc}
\end{aligned}
\]
The Gompertz function2 is a sigmoid function like the logistic, with the difference that it is asymmetric: it leaves its lower limit quickly and approaches its upper limit slowly. It is used as an alternative to the logistic function for the growth of organisms and of populations. It can be derived from the assumption that the relative growth rate, \(f'(x)/f(x)\), declines exponentially with \(x\), as we show below. The practical of Chapter 6 compares it with the logistic function.
The function is
\[
f(x)=a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
\]
where \(a\) is the upper asymptote, \(b\) is a rate and \(c\) is the location of the inflection point. To analyse it we write \(u=e^{-b(x-c)}\), so that \(f(x)=ae^{-u}\). As \(x\to\infty\), \(u\to0\) and \(f(x)\to a\); as \(x\to-\infty\), \(u\) grows without bound and \(f(x)\to0\). The chain rule, with \(du/dx=-bu\), gives
\[
f'(x)=ae^{-u}\times bu=b\,u\,f(x)=b\,f(x)\,\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right),
\]
where the last step uses \(u=-\log\left(f(x)/a\right)\). The relative growth rate is therefore \(f'(x)/f(x)=bu=b\,e^{-b(x-c)}\), an exponential decay. Differentiating once more with the product rule:
\[
f''(x)=b\,f'(x)\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right)-b\,f'(x)
=b\,f'(x)\left[\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right)-1\right].
\]
Since \(f'(x)\) is positive, the second derivative is zero only where \(\log(a/f(x))=1\), that is, where \(f(x)=a/e\). This happens when \(u=1\), at \(x=c\). So the inflection point is at \(x=c\), where the function has reached \(1/e\approx37\%\) of its asymptote (against 50% for the logistic function) and its slope is \(ab/e\). Half of the asymptote is reached later, where \(u=\log 2\), at \(x=c-\log(\log 2)/b\approx c+0.37/b\).
The function is also written as \(a\exp\left(-d\,e^{-bx}\right)\), with \(d=e^{bc}\). In that form the value at zero is \(ae^{-d}\) and the inflection point is at \(x=\log d/b\).

5.5.1 Example: growth of a chick
Suppose that the body mass of a tern chick (g) as a function of its age \(x\) (days) follows a Gompertz function with \(a=110\) g, \(b=0.15\)/day and \(c=5\) days. At hatching the chick weighs
\[
f(0)=110\exp\left(-e^{0.15\times5}\right)=110\exp(-2.117)\approx13.2 \text{ g}.
\]
It grows fastest at an age of 5 days, when it weighs \(110/e\approx40.5\) g and gains \(ab/e=110\times0.15/e\approx6.1\) g/day. It reaches half of its final mass at \(5-\log(\log 2)/0.15\approx7.4\) days, and at 20 days it weighs \(110\exp\left(-e^{-2.25}\right)\approx99\) g. We can verify our math with R:

# Gompertz function: upper asymptote a, rate b and inflection point c
gompertz = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))
}

# Body mass (g) at hatching, at 5 days and at 20 days
gompertz(x = c(0, 5, 20), a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5)

[1] 13.24315 40.46674 98.99617

# Slope at the inflection point: D() and the formula a * b / e
gompertz_derivative = D(expression(a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))), "x")
eval(gompertz_derivative, list(a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5, x = 5))

[1] 6.070011

110 * 0.15 / exp(1)

[1] 6.070011

# The second derivative is zero at the inflection point
gompertz_second = D(gompertz_derivative, "x")
eval(gompertz_second, list(a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5, x = 5))

[1] 0

# Age at which the chick reaches half of its final mass
age_half = 5 - log(log(2)) / 0.15
age_half

[1] 7.443419

gompertz(x = age_half, a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5)

[1] 55







Gompertz function with a = 110, b = 0.15 and c = 5 (solid line) and the logistic function with the same asymptote, the same inflection point and the same maximum slope (dashed line; b = 0.22). Dashed grey lines mark the inflection point and the values a/e and a/2 that the two functions have there.










ImportantPractice: height of a sapling



The height of a sapling (cm) as a function of its age \(x\) (years) is given as \(80\exp\left(-4e^{-0.5x}\right)\). What is its height at \(x=0\)? At which age does it grow fastest, how tall is it then and how fast does it grow?






TipSolution





This is the second form of the function, with \(a=80\) cm, \(d=4\) and \(b=0.5\)/year. At \(x=0\) the height is \(80e^{-4}\approx1.5\) cm. The sapling grows fastest at the inflection point, \(c=\log d/b=\log 4/0.5\approx2.8\) years, when its height is \(a/e\approx29.4\) cm and its growth rate is \(ab/e=80\times0.5/e\approx14.7\) cm/year.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
5.6 Bell-shaped
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2))| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal, symmetric} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{height of the peak (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{width (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{location of the peak (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty \text{ and as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = c \text{ with value } a;\ \text{inflection points at } x = c \pm b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2} \text{ with } \beta_2 < 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The bell-shaped function, or Gaussian curve, describes a response that is highest at one value of the predictor and declines symmetrically on both sides of it. It is used for the abundance or the performance of a species along an environmental gradient, with the location of the peak as the optimum of the species and the width as its tolerance. It is a phenomenological function. Its formula is that of the probability density of the Normal distribution, multiplied by a constant so that the height of the peak is a parameter; here it describes a curve and the area under it has no role.
The function is
\[
f(x)=a\,e^{-(x-c)^2/(2b^2)},
\]
where \(a\) is the height of the peak, \(c\) its location and \(b\) its width. The parameter \(c\) can take any value. The exponent is zero at \(x=c\), where \(f(c)=a\), and it becomes more and more negative on both sides, so \(f(x)\to0\) as \(x\to\infty\) and as \(x\to-\infty\). The chain rule gives
\[
f'(x)=-\frac{x-c}{b^2}\,f(x),
\qquad
f''(x)=\left[\frac{(x-c)^2}{b^2}-1\right]\frac{f(x)}{b^2}.
\]
The slope is positive for \(x<c\), zero at \(x=c\) and negative for \(x>c\), so the maximum is at \(c\). The second derivative is zero where \((x-c)^2=b^2\): the inflection points are at \(x=c\pm b\), where the function equals \(a\,e^{-1/2}\approx0.61a\). The function is concave between them and convex outside. If we solve \(f(x)=a/2\) we find that the function is at half of its height at \(x=c\pm b\sqrt{2\log 2}\approx c\pm1.18b\).
The logarithm of the function is a parabola, so the function is the exponential of a quadratic function, \(e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2}\) with \(\beta_2<0\) (a composition). Comparing the two forms gives
\[
c=-\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}, \qquad b=\sqrt{-\frac{1}{2\beta_2}}, \qquad
a=e^{\beta_0-\beta_1^2/(4\beta_2)}.
\]
For a probability, which cannot exceed 1, the corresponding function is the inverse logit of a quadratic function, \(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left[d-b(x-c)^2\right]\), which is presented in Chapter 5 and used in the practical of Chapter 6.

5.6.1 Example: a diatom along a gradient of pH
Suppose that the abundance of a diatom (cells/mL) in lakes of different pH, \(x\), follows a bell-shaped function with \(a=200\) cells/mL, \(c=6.5\) and \(b=0.8\) units of pH. The abundance is highest, 200 cells/mL, at a pH of 6.5. At the inflection point \(c+b=7.3\) and at a pH of 5 it is
\[
f(7.3)=200\,e^{-1/2}\approx121,
\qquad
f(5)=200\,e^{-(5-6.5)^2/(2\times0.8^2)}=200\,e^{-1.758}\approx34.5
\]
cells/mL. The abundance is at least half of its maximum within \(0.8\sqrt{2\log 2}\approx0.94\) units of pH from the optimum, that is, between a pH of 5.56 and 7.44. We can verify our math with R:

# Bell-shaped function: height a, width b and location c of the peak
bell_shaped = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2))
}

# Abundance (cells/mL) at a pH of 6.5, 7.3 and 5
bell_shaped(x = c(6.5, 7.3, 5), a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5)

[1] 200.00000 121.30613  34.48432

# Values of pH at which the abundance is half of its maximum
half_height = 6.5 + c(-1, 1) * 0.8 * sqrt(2 * log(2))
half_height

[1] 5.558072 7.441928

bell_shaped(x = half_height, a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5)

[1] 100 100

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection points
# c - b and c + b
bell_expression = expression(a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2)))
bell_second = D(D(bell_expression, "x"), "x")
eval(bell_second, list(a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5, x = c(5.7, 7.3)))

[1] -1.110223e-13 -1.110223e-13

# The same curve from the Normal density, rescaled to a height of a
200 * 0.8 * sqrt(2 * pi) * dnorm(x = 5, mean = 6.5, sd = 0.8)

[1] 34.48432







Bell-shaped functions with a peak of height a = 200 at c = 6.5, for a width b = 0.8 (solid line) and b = 0.4 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the peak and the inflection points c − b and c + b of the solid curve.










ImportantPractice: a sedge and the depth of the water table



The expected number of shoots of a sedge in a quadrat is described as \(e^{-1+2x-0.25x^2}\), where \(x\) is the depth of the water table (dm). Write this function as a bell-shaped function: at which depth is the expected number highest, how high is it there, and what is the width \(b\)?






TipSolution





Here \(\beta_0=-1\), \(\beta_1=2\) and \(\beta_2=-0.25\). The peak is at \(c=-\beta_1/(2\beta_2)=-2/(-0.5)=4\) dm. Its height is \(a=e^{\beta_0-\beta_1^2/(4\beta_2)}=e^{-1+4}=e^{3}\approx20.1\) shoots per quadrat, which is also what we obtain by evaluating the function at \(x=4\): \(e^{-1+8-4}=e^{3}\). The width is \(b=\sqrt{-1/(2\beta_2)}=\sqrt{2}\approx1.41\) dm. So the function is \(20.1\,e^{-(x-4)^2/4}\).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.1 Power law
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^b| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{monotonic: increasing when } b > 0,\ \text{decreasing when } b < 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x > 0 \quad (x \geq 0 \text{ when } b > 0) \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y > 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 1 \text{ (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x^b\text{)};\quad
b = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } b > 0;\ \text{grows without bound when } b < 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } b > 0;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } b < 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{none: multiplying } x \text{ by a factor } m \text{ multiplies } y \text{ by } m^b \text{ everywhere} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \log y = \log a + b\log x;\quad y_0\,(x/x_0)^b \text{ with } y_0 = a\,x_0^b
\end{aligned}
\]
The power law describes a response that changes by a constant proportion when the predictor changes by a constant proportion. It is the function of allometry, the study of how the properties of organisms change with their size: the reproductive biomass of plants as a function of the diameter of their stem (Niklas 1993) and the metabolic rate of animals as a function of their body mass (Etienne et al. 2006) are two examples. It is also used for the number of species as a function of the area sampled (Tjørve 2003) and for the fractal properties of landscapes (Halley et al. 2004). A power law is mechanistic when it follows from geometry (the surface of an organism is proportional to the square of its length and its volume to the cube), and many other mechanisms lead to power laws (Mitzenmacher 2003), so the function alone says little about the process behind it.
The function is
\[
f(x)=ax^{b},
\]
where \(b\) is the exponent, which can be positive or negative, and \(a\) is the value of the function at \(x=1\). The two ends depend on the sign of \(b\). When \(b>0\) the function starts at zero and grows without bound; when \(b<0\) it is unbounded as \(x\to0\) and tends to zero as \(x\to\infty\). The power rule gives
\[
f'(x)=ab\,x^{b-1}=b\,\frac{f(x)}{x}, \qquad f''(x)=ab(b-1)\,x^{b-2}.
\]
The function is convex when \(b>1\) or \(b<0\), concave when \(0<b<1\) and a straight line through the origin when \(b=1\). Rearranging the first derivative gives
\[
\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{b}{x},
\]
which says that a small relative change in \(x\) produces a relative change in \(y\) that is \(b\) times as large: an increase of 1% in \(x\) changes \(y\) by about \(b\)%. For a change of any size, \(f(mx)=a(mx)^{b}=m^{b}f(x)\), so multiplying \(x\) by \(m\) multiplies \(y\) by \(m^{b}\), whatever the value of \(x\). It follows that the power law has no characteristic scale and no half-maximum. It has no upper asymptote either; when \(b<0\) it has a horizontal asymptote at zero, which it approaches as \(x\to\infty\). This is the main difference from the exponential function, in which it is a fixed step added to \(x\) that multiplies \(y\) by a constant factor.
Taking logarithms gives \(\log f(x)=\log a+b\log x\): on a plot with two logarithmic axes the power law is a straight line with slope \(b\). The units of \(a\) are awkward, since they depend on \(b\). They become those of \(y\) if we write the function with a reference value \(x_0\) of the predictor,
\[
f(x)=y_0\left(\frac{x}{x_0}\right)^{b}, \qquad y_0=a\,x_0^{b},
\]
where \(y_0\) is the value of the function at \(x=x_0\).

6.1.1 Example: species and area
Suppose that the number of plant species found in a sample of grassland of area \(x\) (ha) is \(f(x)=12x^{0.25}\). The parameter \(a=12\) is the number of species in one hectare and the exponent is \(b=0.25\). In 16 ha and in 10000 ha the function gives
\[
f(16)=12\times16^{0.25}=12\times2=24,
\qquad
f(10000)=12\times10000^{0.25}=12\times10=120
\]
species. Doubling the area multiplies the number of species by \(2^{0.25}\approx1.19\), at any area, and doubling the number of species requires an area that is \(2^{1/0.25}=16\) times larger. The slope at 16 ha is \(b\,f(16)/16=0.25\times24/16=0.375\) species/ha. Written around 16 ha, the function is \(24(x/16)^{0.25}\). We can verify our math with R:

# Power law: value a at x = 1 and exponent b
power_law = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x^b
}

# Number of species in 1, 16 and 10000 ha
power_law(x = c(1, 16, 10000), a = 12, b = 0.25)

[1]  12  24 120

# Factor by which the number of species changes when the area doubles
power_law(x = c(2, 32, 20000), a = 12, b = 0.25) / power_law(x = c(1, 16, 10000), a = 12, b = 0.25)

[1] 1.189207 1.189207 1.189207

# Slope at 16 ha: D() and the formula b * f(x) / x
power_derivative = D(expression(a * x^b), "x")
eval(power_derivative, list(a = 12, b = 0.25, x = 16))

[1] 0.375

0.25 * 24 / 16

[1] 0.375

# The same function written around a reference area of 16 ha, at 100 ha
24 * (100 / 16)^0.25

[1] 37.94733

power_law(x = 100, a = 12, b = 0.25)

[1] 37.94733







Power laws with a = 1 and an exponent b = 0.5 (solid line), b = 1 (dashed line) and b = 2 (dotted line), on the original axes (left) and on logarithmic axes (right), where each of them is a straight line with slope b. The three functions cross at x = 1, where they equal a.










ImportantPractice: leaf area and leaf length



A leaf that is 5 cm long has an area of 20 cm², and a leaf that is 10 cm long has an area of 80 cm². Find the parameters \(a\) and \(b\) of the power law through these two points. Which area does it give for a leaf of 15 cm? What does the value of \(b\) say about the shape of the leaves?






TipSolution





Doubling the length multiplies the area by \(80/20=4\), so \(2^{b}=4\) and \(b=2\). In general, \(b=\log(y_2/y_1)/\log(x_2/x_1)\), the slope of the line on logarithmic axes. From the first point, \(a=20/5^{2}=0.8\) cm²/cm², a number without units. For a leaf of 15 cm the function gives \(0.8\times15^{2}=180\) cm². An exponent of 2 means that the area is proportional to the square of the length, as it is for leaves that keep the same shape as they become larger; \(a=0.8\) is then the area of a leaf as a fraction of the square of its length.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.2 von Bertalanffy
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * (1 - exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating (simple form)};\quad \text{sigmoid (generalised form)} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq c \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptotic size (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{growth rate (inverse units of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{value of } x \text{ at which the size is zero (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a\left(1 - e^{bc}\right),\ \text{slope } ab\,e^{bc} \quad (c \leq 0) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half of the asymptote at } x = c + \log 2/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a - (a - y_0)\,e^{-bx} \text{ with } y_0 = a\left(1 - e^{bc}\right);\quad
a\left(1 - e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^{1/(1-d)} \text{ (generalised form)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The von Bertalanffy function describes the size of an organism as a function of its age. It is the usual growth curve in fisheries and it is a mechanistic function (von Bertalanffy 1938): it follows from a balance between the energy that an organism assimilates and the energy that it spends on maintenance (Essington et al. 2001). In its simple form, which is used for body length, it is a saturating exponential function that is shifted along \(x\). In its generalised form, which is used for body mass, the saturating exponential is raised to a power, and the function becomes sigmoid.
The simple form is
\[
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
\]
where \(a\) is the asymptotic size, \(b\) is the growth rate and \(c\) is the age at which the function is zero. An organism has a positive size at birth, so \(c\) is zero or negative when \(x\) is the age since birth: it is where the curve would start if we extended it backwards, and it is a location parameter with no biological meaning of its own. The properties are those of the saturating exponential function, moved by \(c\). The size at birth is \(f(0)=a\left(1-e^{bc}\right)\), the function tends to \(a\) as \(x\to\infty\), and its derivative,
\[
f'(x)=ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}=b\left(a-f(x)\right),
\]
is positive and decreases with age, so growth is fastest at birth and the function is concave. Half of the asymptotic size is reached at \(x=c+\log 2/b\). Since the size at birth is easier to interpret than \(c\), the function is also written as \(a-(a-y_0)\,e^{-bx}\) with \(y_0=f(0)\).
The generalised form is
\[
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^{1/(1-d)},
\]
where \(d\) is an exponent between 0 and 1, without units. It is the size of an organism that gains mass at a rate proportional to its mass raised to the power \(d\) and loses mass at a rate proportional to its mass; the rate \(b\) is then \(1-d\) times the rate of loss. With \(d=0\) the exponent \(1/(1-d)\) is 1 and we recover the simple form, so the simple form is nested in the generalised one. The value \(d=2/3\) is often used, on the argument that assimilation is proportional to a surface (a length squared) and mass to a volume (a length cubed) (Quinn and Deriso 1999). The exponent is then 3, and the function is the cube of the simple form: if length follows the simple form and mass is proportional to the cube of length, mass follows the generalised form with \(d=2/3\) and the same \(b\) and \(c\).
To find the landmarks of the generalised form we write \(m=1/(1-d)\) and \(u=e^{-b(x-c)}\), so that \(f(x)=a(1-u)^m\) and \(du/dx=-bu\). The chain rule and then the product rule give
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= abm\,u\,(1-u)^{m-1}, \\
f''(x) &= -ab^2m\,u\,(1-u)^{m-2}\left(1-mu\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(m>1\) the slope is zero at \(x=c\), where \(u=1\), and the second derivative changes sign where \(u=1/m\). So the generalised form has an inflection point at
\[
x=c+\frac{\log m}{b}, \qquad \text{with value } a\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)^{m}=a\,d^{\,1/(1-d)}.
\]
For \(d=2/3\) the inflection point is at \(c+\log 3/b\), where the function equals \((2/3)^3a=8a/27\approx0.30\,a\): an organism that follows this function gains mass fastest when it has reached 30% of its final mass.

6.2.1 Example: length and mass of a turtle
Suppose that the length of the carapace of a turtle (cm) as a function of its age \(x\) (years) follows the simple form with \(a=30\) cm, \(b=0.12\)/year and \(c=-1.5\) years. At hatching and at an age of 10 years the carapace is
\[
f(0)=30\left(1-e^{0.12\times(-1.5)}\right)=30\left(1-e^{-0.18}\right)\approx4.9 \text{ cm},
\qquad
f(10)=30\left(1-e^{-0.12\times11.5}\right)\approx22.5 \text{ cm}
\]
long. A hatchling grows by \(ab\,e^{bc}=3.6\,e^{-0.18}\approx3.0\) cm/year, and the turtle reaches half of its final length at \(-1.5+\log 2/0.12\approx4.3\) years.
Suppose also that the body mass of the turtle is proportional to the cube of the length of its carapace and approaches 2500 g. Body mass then follows the generalised form with \(a=2500\) g, \(d=2/3\) and the same \(b\) and \(c\). At 10 years the turtle weighs \(2500\times(22.5/30)^3\approx1048\) g. It gains mass fastest at an age of \(-1.5+\log 3/0.12\approx7.7\) years, when it weighs \(8\times2500/27\approx741\) g. We can verify our math with R:

# von Bertalanffy function: asymptotic size a, growth rate b, age c at which the size
# is zero and exponent d (d = 0 gives the simple form)
von_bertalanffy = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0, d = 0) {
  a * (1 - exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / (1 - d))
}

# Length of the carapace (cm) at hatching and at 10 years
von_bertalanffy(x = c(0, 10), a = 30, b = 0.12, c = -1.5)

[1]  4.941894 22.452643

# The same written with the length at hatching
30 - (30 - 30 * (1 - exp(-0.18))) * exp(-0.12 * c(0, 10))

[1]  4.941894 22.452643

# Growth of a hatchling (cm/year) and age at half of the final length
30 * 0.12 * exp(0.12 * -1.5)

[1] 3.006973

-1.5 + log(2) / 0.12

[1] 4.276227

# Body mass (g) at 10 years, with d = 2/3
von_bertalanffy(x = 10, a = 2500, b = 0.12, c = -1.5, d = 2 / 3)

[1] 1048.042

# Age and body mass at the inflection point
age_inflection = -1.5 + log(3) / 0.12
age_inflection

[1] 7.655102

von_bertalanffy(x = age_inflection, a = 2500, b = 0.12, c = -1.5, d = 2 / 3)

[1] 740.7407

8 * 2500 / 27

[1] 740.7407
