Dashed grey lines mark the inflection point of the generalised form, c + log(3)/b, and its value there, 8/27 of the asymptote.










ImportantPractice: length of a lizard



A paper gives the length of a lizard (cm, from snout to vent) as a function of its age \(x\) (years) as \(12-(12-3)\,e^{-0.4x}\). Find the parameters \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) of the simple von Bertalanffy function, with their units. At which age does the lizard reach 90% of its final length?






TipSolution





The function is written with the length at hatching, \(y_0=3\) cm, so \(a=12\) cm and \(b=0.4\)/year. The parameter \(c\) follows from \(y_0=a\left(1-e^{bc}\right)\): \(e^{0.4c}=1-3/12=0.75\), so \(c=\log(0.75)/0.4\approx-0.72\) years. The function reaches 90% of its asymptote when \(e^{-b(x-c)}=0.1\), that is, at \(x=c+\log(10)/b\approx-0.72+5.76=5.04\) years.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.3 Shepherd
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x / (b + x^c)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{increasing when } c < 1;\ \text{saturating when } c = 1;\ \text{unimodal when } c > 1 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a \text{ (units of } y \text{ times units of } x^{c-1}\text{)};\quad
b \text{ (units of } x^c\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } c < 1;\ f(x) \to a \text{ when } c = 1;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } c > 1 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c > 1,\ \text{maximum at } x = \left(b/(c-1)\right)^{1/c} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{sx}{1 + (x/k)^c},\ \text{with } s = a/b \text{ and } k = b^{1/c}
\end{aligned}
\]
The Shepherd function is a Michaelis–Menten function in which the \(x\) of the denominator is raised to a power. It is used for the output of a population (recruits, seeds, the adults of the next generation) as a function of its density, when the strength of the competition among individuals is to be estimated from the data (Maynard Smith and Slatkin 1973; Brännström and Sumpter 2005). The exponent \(c\) sets that strength. With \(c=1\) the function is the Michaelis–Menten function and the output levels off. With \(c<1\) the output keeps increasing with density, and with \(c>1\) it declines at high density, as it does for the Ricker function; population ecologists call the two cases undercompensating and overcompensating density dependence. In fisheries the function generalises the Beverton–Holt curve, and it can be derived from a mortality of the young fish that depends on the initial size of their cohort (Quinn and Deriso 1999).
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x^{c}},
\]
where \(c\) is the exponent and \(a\) and \(b\) are positive. The units of \(a\) and \(b\) depend on \(c\), which makes them hard to interpret, so we first look for landmarks. For small \(x\) the term \(x^c\) is negligible next to \(b\) and \(f(x)\approx(a/b)\,x\): the initial slope is \(a/b\). For large \(x\) the term \(b\) is negligible next to \(x^c\) and \(f(x)\approx ax^{1-c}\), which grows without bound when \(c<1\), equals \(a\) when \(c=1\) and tends to zero when \(c>1\). The quotient rule gives
\[
f'(x)=\frac{a\left(b+x^{c}\right)-ax\times cx^{c-1}}{\left(b+x^{c}\right)^2}
=\frac{a\left[b-(c-1)\,x^{c}\right]}{\left(b+x^{c}\right)^2}.
\]
When \(c\le1\) the numerator is positive for every \(x\) and the function increases throughout. When \(c>1\) the numerator is zero where \(x^c=b/(c-1)\), so the function has a maximum at
\[
x_{\max}=\left(\frac{b}{c-1}\right)^{1/c},
\qquad
f(x_{\max})=\frac{a\,(c-1)}{bc}\,x_{\max},
\]
where the value follows from replacing \(x^c\) by \(b/(c-1)\) in the denominator.
The function is easier to read with the initial slope \(s=a/b\) and the scale \(k=b^{1/c}\) as parameters, which we obtain by dividing the numerator and the denominator by \(b\):
\[
f(x)=\frac{sx}{1+(x/k)^{c}}.
\]
In this reparameterisation \(k\) has the units of \(x\) and \(s\) those of \(y\) per unit of \(x\). At \(x=k\) the denominator equals 2 whatever the value of \(c\), so \(k\) is the density at which the output is half of what the initial slope alone would give, \(sk/2\). The exponent then decides what happens beyond \(k\), and the maximum for \(c>1\) is at \(k\,(c-1)^{-1/c}\).

6.3.1 Example: flour beetles in a jar
Suppose that the number of adult beetles that emerge from a jar of flour, as a function of the number of eggs \(x\) that were laid in it, is \(f(x)=8000x/(10000+x^2)\), a Shepherd function with \(c=2\). The initial slope is \(a/b=0.8\) adults per egg, the fraction of the eggs that become adults when there is no competition, and the scale is \(k=\sqrt{10000}=100\) eggs. The number of adults is highest at
\[
x_{\max}=\left(\frac{10000}{2-1}\right)^{1/2}=100 \text{ eggs},
\qquad
f(100)=\frac{8000\times100}{10000+10000}=40 \text{ adults},
\]
which is \(sk/2=0.8\times100/2\). With 300 eggs the jar produces \(8000\times300/(10000+90000)=24\) adults. With \(c=1\) and the same initial slope and scale the function is the Michaelis–Menten function \(80x/(100+x)\), which gives 40 adults for 100 eggs as well and 60 adults for 300 eggs. We can verify our math with R:

# Shepherd function: parameters a and b and exponent c
shepherd = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x^c)
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of numbers of eggs
egg_grid = seq(0, 1000, by = 0.01)
adult_values = shepherd(egg_grid, a = 8000, b = 10000, c = 2)
egg_grid[which.max(adult_values)]

[1] 100

max(adult_values)

[1] 40

# Adults from 100 and from 300 eggs
shepherd(x = c(100, 300), a = 8000, b = 10000, c = 2)

[1] 40 24

# The same function written with the initial slope s = 0.8 and the scale k = 100
0.8 * c(100, 300) / (1 + (c(100, 300) / 100)^2)

[1] 40 24

# With c = 1 it is a Michaelis–Menten function with asymptote 80 and half-maximum 100
shepherd(x = c(100, 300), a = 80, b = 100, c = 1)

[1] 40 60







Shepherd functions with an initial slope s = 0.8 and a scale k = 100, for c = 0.5 (dotted line), c = 1 (dashed line; a Michaelis–Menten function) and c = 2 (solid line). Dashed grey lines mark the scale k and the value sk/2 = 40 that the three functions have there.










ImportantPractice: biomass of a crop and sowing density



The biomass of a crop (kg/m²) as a function of the density at which it was sown, \(x\) (thousands of seeds/m²), is described by \(f(x)=24x/(16+x^3)\). What is the initial slope of this Shepherd function? At which sowing density is the biomass highest, and how high is it there? What does the function do at very high densities?






TipSolution





The initial slope is \(a/b=24/16=1.5\) kg per thousand seeds. The exponent is \(c=3\), which is larger than 1, so the function has a maximum at \(x_{\max}=\left(b/(c-1)\right)^{1/c}=(16/2)^{1/3}=2\) thousand seeds/m², where it equals \(24\times2/(16+8)=2\) kg/m². For large \(x\) the function is close to \(ax^{1-c}=24/x^2\), so the biomass tends to zero at very high densities.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.4 Hassell
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x / (b + x)^c| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{increasing when } c < 1;\ \text{saturating when } c = 1;\ \text{unimodal when } c > 1 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a \text{ (units of } y \text{ times units of } x^{c-1}\text{)};\quad
b \text{ (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b^c \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } c < 1;\ f(x) \to a \text{ when } c = 1;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } c > 1 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c > 1,\ \text{maximum at } x = b/(c-1) \text{ and inflection point at } x = 2b/(c-1) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{sx}{(1 + x/b)^c},\ \text{with } s = a/b^c \text{ the initial slope}
\end{aligned}
\]
The Hassell function is a Michaelis–Menten function in which the whole denominator is raised to a power. Hassell (1975) proposed it for the density dependence of populations with one generation per year, and it is used in the same way as the Shepherd function, from which it differs in where the exponent is placed (see also Brännström and Sumpter 2005). The exponent \(c\) again sets the strength of the competition: the output keeps increasing with density when \(c<1\), levels off when \(c=1\) and declines at high density when \(c>1\). The function is mostly used phenomenologically, to let the data decide among these three cases.
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{ax}{(b+x)^{c}},
\]
where \(c\) is the exponent, \(b\) has the units of \(x\) and \(a\) has units that depend on \(c\). For small \(x\) the denominator is close to \(b^c\), so the initial slope is \(a/b^c\). For large \(x\) the denominator is close to \(x^c\) and \(f(x)\approx ax^{1-c}\), which gives the same three cases as for the Shepherd function. The quotient rule, with the chain rule for the denominator, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{a\,(b+x)^{c}-ax\times c\,(b+x)^{c-1}}{(b+x)^{2c}}
=\frac{a\left[b-(c-1)\,x\right]}{(b+x)^{c+1}}, \\
f''(x) &= \frac{ac\left[(c-1)\,x-2b\right]}{(b+x)^{c+2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
When \(c\le1\) the slope is positive for every \(x\). When \(c>1\) the numerator of the first derivative is zero at
\[
x_{\max}=\frac{b}{c-1},
\qquad
f(x_{\max})=\frac{a\,(c-1)^{c-1}}{c^{\,c}\,b^{\,c-1}},
\]
which is a maximum, and the numerator of the second derivative is zero at \(x=2b/(c-1)\), an inflection point on the way down. As for the Ricker function, the inflection point is at twice the location of the maximum. The value of the maximum follows from \(b+x_{\max}=bc/(c-1)\); for \(c=2\) it is \(a/(4b)\) and for \(c=3\) it is \(4a/(27b^2)\).
The resemblance to the Ricker function has a reason. With the initial slope as a parameter the function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{sx}{(1+x/b)^{c}}, \qquad s=\frac{a}{b^{c}},
\]
and if we let \(c\) grow while we keep the ratio \(c/b\) at a fixed value \(\beta\), the term \((1+\beta x/c)^{-c}\) tends to \(e^{-\beta x}\). So the Hassell function has the Michaelis–Menten function at one end of its range (\(c=1\)) and approaches the Ricker function \(sxe^{-\beta x}\) at the other.

6.4.1 Example: larvae that compete for food
Suppose that the number of adult flies that emerge per gram of food, as a function of the density of larvae \(x\) (larvae/g), is \(f(x)=800x/(10+x)^3\). The exponent is \(c=3\) and \(b=10\) larvae/g. The initial slope is \(a/b^c=800/1000=0.8\) adults per larva. The number of adults is highest at
\[
x_{\max}=\frac{10}{3-1}=5 \text{ larvae/g},
\qquad
f(5)=\frac{800\times5}{15^3}=\frac{4\times800}{27\times10^2}\approx1.19 \text{ adults/g},
\]
and the inflection point is at \(2\times10/(3-1)=10\) larvae/g, where the function gives \(800\times10/20^3=1\) adult/g. At 40 larvae/g it gives \(800\times40/50^3\approx0.26\) adults/g. We can verify our math with R:

# Hassell function: parameters a and b and exponent c
hassell = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x)^c
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of densities
larva_grid = seq(0, 200, by = 0.001)
adult_values = hassell(larva_grid, a = 800, b = 10, c = 3)
larva_grid[which.max(adult_values)]

[1] 5

max(adult_values)

[1] 1.185185

# Adults per gram at 5, 10 and 40 larvae/g
hassell(x = c(5, 10, 40), a = 800, b = 10, c = 3)

[1] 1.185185 1.000000 0.256000

# Initial slope: D() and the formula a / b^c
hassell_derivative = D(expression(a * x / (b + x)^c), "x")
eval(hassell_derivative, list(a = 800, b = 10, c = 3, x = 0))

[1] 0.8

800 / 10^3

[1] 0.8

# The second derivative is zero at the inflection point
eval(D(hassell_derivative, "x"), list(a = 800, b = 10, c = 3, x = 10))

[1] 0

# With a larger exponent and the same c / b = 0.3 and initial slope, the function
# approaches the Ricker function 0.8 * x * exp(-0.3 * x): values at 5 larvae/g
0.8 * 5 / (1 + 0.3 * 5 / c(3, 30, 3000))^c(3, 30, 3000)

[1] 1.1851852 0.9255098 0.8928553

0.8 * 5 * exp(-0.3 * 5)

[1] 0.8925206







Hassell functions with an initial slope s = 0.8 and a ratio c/b = 0.3, for c = 3 (solid line; b = 10) and c = 30 (dashed line; b = 100), and the Ricker function with the same initial slope and a rate of 0.3 (dotted line), which the Hassell function approaches as c grows. Dashed grey lines mark the maximum and the inflection point of the solid curve, at b/(c − 1) = 5 and 2b/(c − 1) = 10.










ImportantPractice: a Hassell function with a given initial slope



A Hassell function has \(b=12\) plants/m² and \(c=4\). Where are its maximum and its inflection point? Which value of \(a\) gives an initial slope of 0.5 seeds per plant, and how high is the maximum then?






TipSolution





The maximum is at \(b/(c-1)=12/3=4\) plants/m² and the inflection point at twice that density, \(2b/(c-1)=8\) plants/m². The initial slope is \(a/b^c\), so \(a=0.5\times12^4=10368\). The maximum is then \(f(4)=10368\times4/16^4=41472/65536\approx0.63\) seeds/m², which is also what the formula gives: \(a\,(c-1)^{c-1}/(c^{\,c}b^{\,c-1})=10368\times27/(256\times1728)\approx0.63\).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.5 Generalised Ricker
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal, of adjustable width} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{height of the peak (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{location of the peak (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0;\ \text{slope } 0 \text{ when } c > 1,\ ae/b \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = b \text{ with value } a;\ \text{inflection points at } x = b\left(1 \pm 1/\sqrt{c}\right) \text{ (only the upper one when } c \leq 1\text{)} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a'x^{c}e^{-cx/b} \text{ with } a' = a\,(e/b)^{c};\quad
\text{with } c = 1,\ \text{the Ricker function } (ae/b)\,x\,e^{-x/b}
\end{aligned}
\]
The generalised Ricker function describes a response with a single peak whose location, height and width are three separate parameters. In the Ricker function one parameter controls both where the peak is and how fast the function declines beyond it, so a peak that is far from zero is necessarily wide; the exponent of the generalised function removes that link. Persson et al. (1998) used it for the attack rate of a predator as a function of its body mass, and in fisheries it has been proposed for the number of recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock (Quinn and Deriso 1999). It is a phenomenological function. Chapter 5 uses it for the number of tadpoles killed as a function of their body length. Bellows (1981) proposed another generalisation of the Ricker function, in which the power is placed inside the exponential.
The function is
\[
f(x)=a\left[\frac{x}{b}\,e^{1-x/b}\right]^{c},
\]
where \(a\) is the height of the peak, \(b\) is its location and \(c\) is a positive exponent. The term in brackets is a Ricker function that is written so that its maximum is at \(x=b\) and has a value of 1. The function is zero at \(x=0\), and it tends to zero as \(x\to\infty\) because the exponential dominates the power of \(x\). The derivative is easiest to find from the logarithm of the function, \(\log f(x)=\log a+c\left[\log(x/b)+1-x/b\right]\), whose derivative is \(f'(x)/f(x)\):
\[
f'(x)=c\,f(x)\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{b}\right).
\]
The slope is positive for \(x<b\), zero at \(x=b\) and negative for \(x>b\), whatever the value of \(c\): the maximum is at \(x=b\), where the term in brackets equals 1 and \(f(b)=a\). Differentiating once more with the product rule gives
\[
f''(x)=c\,f(x)\left[c\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right],
\]
which is zero where \(\sqrt{c}\,\left|1-x/b\right|=1\). So the inflection points are at
\[
x=b\left(1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}\right),
\]
one on each side of the peak when \(c>1\). The distance between them, \(2b/\sqrt{c}\), is a measure of the width of the peak: a peak that is half as wide needs an exponent that is four times as large. When \(c\le1\) the lower value is zero or negative and is not an inflection point (with \(c=1\) it is \(x=0\), where the second derivative is \(-2ae/b^2\) and not zero), so the only inflection point is the upper one. With \(c=1\) it is at \(2b\), as for the Ricker function. Near its peak the function is close to the bell-shaped function with height \(a\), location \(b\) and width \(b/\sqrt{c}\).
With \(c=1\) the function is \((ae/b)\,xe^{-x/b}\), a Ricker function with an initial slope \(ae/b\) and a rate \(1/b\). For any \(c\) the function can be multiplied out to \(a'x^{c}e^{-cx/b}\) with \(a'=a\,(e/b)^{c}\), a power of \(x\) multiplied by an exponential, which is the form in which it is often printed.

6.5.1 Example: attack rate and body mass of a perch
Suppose that the volume of water that a perch clears of zooplankton (L/hour), as a function of its body mass \(x\) (g), follows a generalised Ricker function with \(a=3\) L/hour, \(b=20\) g and \(c=4\). The attack rate is highest, 3 L/hour, for a perch of 20 g. The inflection points are at \(20\,(1\pm1/\sqrt{4})\), that is, at 10 and 30 g, where the function gives
\[
f(10)=3\left[0.5\,e^{0.5}\right]^{4}\approx1.39,
\qquad
f(30)=3\left[1.5\,e^{-0.5}\right]^{4}\approx2.06
\]
L/hour. The function is asymmetric: it rises more steeply than it falls. With \(c=1\) and the same \(a\) and \(b\) it would be the Ricker function with an initial slope \(ae/b\approx0.41\) L/hour/g, which gives 2.47 L/hour at 10 g and 2.73 at 30 g, a much wider peak. We can verify our math with R:

# Generalised Ricker function: height a and location b of the peak, exponent c
generalised_ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1) {
  a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c
}

# Attack rate (L/hour) at 10, 20 and 30 g
generalised_ricker(x = c(10, 20, 30), a = 3, b = 20, c = 4)

[1] 1.385448 3.000000 2.055405

# Location of the maximum on a fine grid of body mass
mass_grid = seq(0, 100, by = 0.001)
mass_grid[which.max(generalised_ricker(mass_grid, a = 3, b = 20, c = 4))]

[1] 20

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection points
ricker_expression = expression(a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c)
ricker_second = D(D(ricker_expression, "x"), "x")
eval(ricker_second, list(a = 3, b = 20, c = 4, x = c(10, 30)))

[1] -5.204170e-18 -1.301043e-18

# With c = 1 it is a Ricker function with initial slope a * e / b and rate 1 / b
generalised_ricker(x = c(10, 30), a = 3, b = 20, c = 1)

[1] 2.473082 2.729388

(3 * exp(1) / 20) * c(10, 30) * exp(-c(10, 30) / 20)

[1] 2.473082 2.729388







Generalised Ricker functions with a peak of height a = 3 at b = 20, for an exponent c = 1 (dotted line; a Ricker function), c = 4 (solid line) and c = 16 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the peak and the inflection points of the solid curve, at 10 and 30.










ImportantPractice: reading the exponent from a plot



The activity of a ground beetle (captures per trap per night) as a function of temperature is highest at 15 °C, where it is 50 captures, and a plot of the data suggests that the curve changes from convex to concave at 12 °C and back to convex at 18 °C. Find the parameters \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) of a generalised Ricker function with these properties.






TipSolution





The height of the peak is \(a=50\) captures per trap per night and its location is \(b=15\) °C. The two values at which the curvature changes are the inflection points, \(b\,(1\pm1/\sqrt{c})\). Their distance from the peak is \(b/\sqrt{c}=3\) °C, so \(\sqrt{c}=15/3=5\) and \(c=25\). These are the values that we would use as starting values when fitting the function to the data (see Starting values by eye).

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.6 Non-rectangular hyperbola
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|(s + p_max - sqrt((s + p_max)^2 - 4 * theta * s * p_max)) / (2 * theta)|,\ \text{with } \texttt{s = alpha * x} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating, with a bend of adjustable sharpness} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < p_{\max} \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad \alpha = \text{initial slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
p_{\max} = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)}; \\
&\quad \theta = \text{sharpness of the bend (no units)},\ 0 < \theta \leq 1 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } \alpha \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to p_{\max},\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{at } x = p_{\max}/\alpha \text{ the function equals } p_{\max}/\left(1 + \sqrt{1 - \theta}\right) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{the smaller root } y \text{ of } \theta y^2 - (\alpha x + p_{\max})\,y + \alpha x\,p_{\max} = 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The non-rectangular hyperbola describes the rate of photosynthesis of a leaf as a function of the light that it receives. It is a saturating function with three parameters: the initial slope, the asymptote and the sharpness of the bend between the two. It is derived from principles of plant physiology (Thornley 2002), so it is a mechanistic function, and its parameters have their own symbols in that field: \(\alpha\) is the efficiency with which the leaf uses light when light is scarce, \(p_{\max}\) is the rate of photosynthesis when light is abundant and \(\theta\) is the sharpness. We keep these symbols here. In the terms of the Michaelis–Menten function, \(p_{\max}\) is the asymptote \(a\) and \(\alpha\) is the initial slope \(a/b\).
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{\alpha x+p_{\max}-\sqrt{\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)^2-4\,\theta\,\alpha x\,p_{\max}}}{2\,\theta},
\]
where \(x\) is the light received by the leaf. The formula is the smaller of the two solutions of a quadratic equation in \(y=f(x)\),
\[
\theta\,y^2-\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)y+\alpha x\,p_{\max}=0,
\]
and the properties of the function are easier to derive from this equation than from the formula. If we move the term \((1-\theta)\,y^2\) to the right-hand side, the left-hand side can be factorised:
\[
\left(\alpha x-y\right)\left(p_{\max}-y\right)=(1-\theta)\,y^2 .
\]
The two factors on the left are the distances from \(y\) to the straight line \(\alpha x\) and to the plateau \(p_{\max}\). This form shows the two extremes of the function. When \(\theta=1\) the right-hand side is zero, so one of the two factors has to be zero: \(y\) is either on the line or on the plateau, and the smaller root is \(\min(\alpha x,p_{\max})\), a hockey stick function with a breakpoint at \(x=p_{\max}/\alpha\). When \(\theta=0\) the quadratic term of the equation vanishes and what remains is \(\alpha x\,p_{\max}=\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)y\), that is,
\[
y=\frac{\alpha x\,p_{\max}}{\alpha x+p_{\max}}=\frac{p_{\max}\,x}{p_{\max}/\alpha+x},
\]
a Michaelis–Menten function with an asymptote \(p_{\max}\) and a half-maximum \(p_{\max}/\alpha\). (The formula itself cannot be evaluated at \(\theta=0\), as it divides by zero; the Michaelis–Menten function is its limit as \(\theta\to0\).) Both functions are therefore nested in the non-rectangular hyperbola, and values of \(\theta\) between 0 and 1 give curves between them.
The limits follow from the same form. At \(x=0\) the equation is satisfied by \(y=0\). For small \(x\) and \(y\), the term \(y^2\) is negligible and \(p_{\max}-y\approx p_{\max}\), so \(y\approx\alpha x\): the initial slope is \(\alpha\) for every \(\theta\). Dividing both sides by \(\alpha x\) gives \((1-y/(\alpha x))(p_{\max}-y)=(1-\theta)\,y^2/(\alpha x)\), whose right-hand side tends to zero as \(x\to\infty\) since \(y\) stays below \(p_{\max}\), so \(f(x)\to p_{\max}\).
The parameter \(\theta\) can be read at one particular value of \(x\). At \(x=p_{\max}/\alpha\), where the line \(\alpha x\) crosses the plateau, the equation becomes \(\theta y^2-2p_{\max}\,y+p_{\max}^2=0\), and its smaller root is
\[
f\left(\frac{p_{\max}}{\alpha}\right)=\frac{p_{\max}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)}{\theta}
=\frac{p_{\max}}{1+\sqrt{1-\theta}} .
\]
At this value of \(x\) the function is at half of its asymptote when \(\theta=0\), at two thirds when \(\theta=0.75\) and on the asymptote when \(\theta=1\). The sharpness is hard to estimate from data (Thornley 2002), because it only affects the function around the bend.
Leaves also respire, so that their net exchange of carbon dioxide is negative in the dark. This is described by subtracting the rate of respiration from the function, which is a shift along \(y\).

6.6.1 Example: photosynthesis of a leaf
Suppose that a leaf has \(\alpha=0.05\) µmol of carbon dioxide per µmol of light, \(p_{\max}=20\) µmol/m²/s and \(\theta=0.75\), with the light \(x\) in µmol/m²/s. The line and the plateau cross at \(x=p_{\max}/\alpha=20/0.05=400\) µmol/m²/s, where the rate of photosynthesis is
\[
f(400)=\frac{20}{1+\sqrt{1-0.75}}=\frac{20}{1.5}\approx13.3 \text{ µmol/m}^2\text{/s}.
\]
At \(x=100\) we have \(\alpha x=5\), and the formula gives
\[
f(100)=\frac{5+20-\sqrt{25^2-4\times0.75\times5\times20}}{2\times0.75}
=\frac{25-\sqrt{325}}{1.5}\approx4.65 \text{ µmol/m}^2\text{/s},
\]
which lies between the 4 µmol/m²/s of the Michaelis–Menten function (\(5\times20/25\)) and the 5 of the hockey stick. We can verify our math with R:

# Non-rectangular hyperbola: initial slope alpha, asymptote p_max and sharpness theta
non_rectangular = function(x, alpha = 1, p_max = 1, theta = 0.5) {
  (alpha * x + p_max - sqrt((alpha * x + p_max)^2 - 4 * theta * alpha * x * p_max)) /
    (2 * theta)
}

# Photosynthesis at a light of 100, 400 and 1500
light_values = c(100, 400, 1500)
non_rectangular(x = light_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.75)

[1]  4.648162 13.333333 18.487920

# Value at x = p_max / alpha from the formula derived on paper
20 / (1 + sqrt(1 - 0.75))

[1] 13.33333

# A sharpness close to 0 gives the Michaelis–Menten function
non_rectangular(x = light_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.000001)

[1]  4.000001 10.000003 15.789476

20 * light_values / (20 / 0.05 + light_values)

[1]  4.00000 10.00000 15.78947

# A sharpness of 1 gives the hockey stick function
non_rectangular(x = light_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 1)

[1]  5 20 20

pmin(0.05 * light_values, 20)

[1]  5 20 20

# Initial slope: finite-difference slope at zero with a small step
(non_rectangular(x = 0.001, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.75) - 0) / 0.001

[1] 0.04999997







Non-rectangular hyperbolas with an initial slope α = 0.05 and an asymptote p_max = 20, for a sharpness θ close to 0 (dotted line; a Michaelis–Menten function), θ = 0.75 (solid line) and θ = 1 (dashed line; a hockey stick function). Dashed grey lines mark the asymptote and the value of x at which the line αx crosses it, p_max/α = 400.










ImportantPractice: the sharpness of a light response



The photosynthesis of a leaf approaches 30 µmol/m²/s in bright light and increases by 0.06 µmol of carbon dioxide per µmol of light when light is scarce. At which light does the straight line of the initial slope cross the asymptote? At that light the leaf is measured to photosynthesise at 80% of its asymptote. Which sharpness \(\theta\) does this correspond to?






TipSolution





The line crosses the asymptote at \(x=p_{\max}/\alpha=30/0.06=500\) µmol/m²/s. There the function equals \(p_{\max}/\left(1+\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)\), so \(1/\left(1+\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)=0.8\). This gives \(\sqrt{1-\theta}=1/0.8-1=0.25\) and \(\theta=1-0.25^2=0.9375\). A Michaelis–Menten function would be at 50% of its asymptote at this light and a hockey stick function at 100%.

title: Deterministic functions
text:
6.7 Richards
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, of adjustable asymmetry} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \text{ when } d > 0;\quad x \geq c + \log(-d)/b \text{ when } -1 \leq d < 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{inflection point (units of } x\text{)};\quad d = \text{shape (no units)},\ d \geq -1,\ d \neq 0 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/\left(1 + d\,e^{bc}\right)^{1/d} \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \text{ when } d > 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a\,(1 + d)^{-1/d} \text{ and slope } ab\,(1 + d)^{-1/d - 1} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{logistic } (d = 1);\ \text{Gompertz } (d \to 0);\ \text{saturating exponential } (d = -1)
\end{aligned}
\]
The Richards function is a family of growth curves with an upper asymptote, in which a fourth parameter sets how asymmetric the curve is. Richards (1959) proposed it as a flexible function for the growth of plants, and it is used when neither the logistic nor the Gompertz function describes the data well, for example for the growth of individual plants (Damgaard et al. 2002). Its interest for this book is that it contains several of the functions of this supplement as special cases (Haefner 1996; Damgaard et al. 2002), so it shows how they are related. In general it is a phenomenological function, although particular values of the shape parameter give functions that have a mechanism. Other generalisations of the logistic function exist: Emlen (1996) raised \(x\) to a power inside the exponential, and Schnute (1981) proposed a growth function that is more general still.
The function is
\[
f(x)=\frac{a}{\left[1+d\,e^{-b(x-c)}\right]^{1/d}},
\]
where \(a\) is the upper asymptote, \(b\) is a rate, \(c\) is the location of the inflection point and \(d\) is the shape parameter. As for the Gompertz function we write \(u=e^{-b(x-c)}\), so that \(f(x)=a\,(1+du)^{-1/d}\). As \(x\to\infty\), \(u\to0\) and \(f(x)\to a\). When \(d>0\), \(u\) grows without bound as \(x\to-\infty\) and \(f(x)\to0\). When \(d\) is negative the term \(1+du\) reaches zero at \(u=-1/d\), so the function starts from zero at \(x=c+\log(-d)/b\) and is used from that value onwards.
The special cases follow from the value of \(d\):



Shape parameter
Function
Value at the inflection point




\(d=1\)
Logistic, \(a/\left(1+e^{-b(x-c)}\right)\)
\(a/2\)


\(d\to0\)
Gompertz, \(a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)\)
\(a/e\approx0.37\,a\)


\(d=-1/3\)
Generalised von Bertalanffy with an exponent of 3
\(8a/27\approx0.30\,a\)


\(d=-1\)
Saturating exponential, \(a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)\)
0 (no inflection point)



The cases \(d=1\) and \(d=-1\) are found by substituting the value in the formula. For the Gompertz function we use the limit that defines the exponential function, \((1+du)^{1/d}\to e^{u}\) as \(d\to0\). For \(d=-1/3\) the function is \(a\left(1-\tfrac{1}{3}u\right)^{3}\), and since \(\tfrac{1}{3}e^{-b(x-c)}=e^{-b(x-c')}\) with \(c'=c-\log 3/b\), this is the generalised von Bertalanffy function that starts at \(c'\). Note that the parameters \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) keep their meaning along the whole family.
The chain rule, with \(du/dx=-bu\), gives
\[
f'(x)=ab\,u\,(1+du)^{-1/d-1}=\frac{b}{d}\,f(x)\left[1-\left(\frac{f(x)}{a}\right)^{d}\right],
\]
where the last step uses \(1+du=\left(a/f(x)\right)^{d}\). For \(d=1\) this is the derivative of the logistic function, \(b\,f(x)\left(1-f(x)/a\right)\). Differentiating the last expression once more with the product rule:
\[
f''(x)=\frac{b}{d}\,f'(x)\left[1-(1+d)\left(\frac{f(x)}{a}\right)^{d}\right].
\]
Since \(f'(x)\) is positive, the second derivative is zero only where \(\left(f(x)/a\right)^{d}=1/(1+d)\). This happens where \(1+du=1+d\), that is, where \(u=1\) and \(x=c\). So for every \(d>-1\) the inflection point is at \(x=c\), and
\[
f(c)=a\,(1+d)^{-1/d}, \qquad f'(c)=ab\,(1+d)^{-1/d-1}.
\]
The shape parameter therefore decides at which fraction of the asymptote the function is steepest: the fraction increases with \(d\), from zero at \(d=-1\) through one half at \(d=1\) towards one for large \(d\). As for the other exponents of this group, \(d\) is hard to estimate from data.

6.7.1 Example: growth of an annual plant
Suppose that the dry mass of a plant (g) as a function of the time since emergence \(x\) (days) follows a Richards function with \(a=50\) g, \(b=0.1\)/day, \(c=30\) days and \(d=0.5\). The plant grows fastest at 30 days, when its mass is
\[
f(30)=50\times(1+0.5)^{-1/0.5}=\frac{50}{1.5^2}\approx22.2 \text{ g},
\]
that is, 44% of its final mass, and it then grows by \(ab\,(1+d)^{-1/d-1}=50\times0.1/1.5^3\approx1.48\) g/day. At emergence its mass is \(50/\left(1+0.5\,e^{3}\right)^{2}\approx0.41\) g, and after 60 days it is \(50/\left(1+0.5\,e^{-3}\right)^{2}\approx47.6\) g. With the same \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\), a logistic function would give 25 g at 30 days and a Gompertz function \(50/e\approx18.4\) g. We can verify our math with R:

# Richards function: upper asymptote a, rate b, inflection point c and shape d
richards = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0, d = 1) {
  a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)
}

# Dry mass (g) at emergence, at 30 days and at 60 days
richards(x = c(0, 30, 60), a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.5)

[1]  0.4100285 22.2222222 47.6006078

# Slope at the inflection point: D() and the formula a * b * (1 + d)^(-1 / d - 1)
richards_derivative = D(expression(a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)), "x")
eval(richards_derivative, list(a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.5, x = 30))

[1] 1.481481

50 * 0.1 * (1 + 0.5)^(-1 / 0.5 - 1)

[1] 1.481481

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection point
eval(D(richards_derivative, "x"), list(a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.5, x = 30))

[1] 0

# Special cases at 10, 30 and 45 days: d = 1 is the logistic function
days = c(10, 30, 45)
richards(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 1)

[1]  5.960146 25.000000 40.878724

logistic(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30)

[1]  5.960146 25.000000 40.878724

# A shape parameter close to 0 gives the Gompertz function
richards(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.000001)

[1]  0.03089979 18.39398126 40.00053665

gompertz(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30)

[1]  0.03089895 18.39397206 40.00053565

# d = -1 is the saturating exponential function that starts at c (here from 30 days)
richards(x = c(30, 45, 60), a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = -1)

[1]  0.00000 38.84349 47.51065

saturating_exponential(x = c(30, 45, 60) - 30, a = 50, b = 0.1)

[1]  0.00000 38.84349 47.51065







Richards functions with a = 50, b = 0.1 and c = 30, for a shape parameter d close to 0 (dotted line; a Gompertz function), d = 1 (dashed line; a logistic function) and d = 4 (solid line). The dashed grey line marks the inflection point, which is at x = c for the three functions; the value of the function there increases with d.










ImportantPractice: the shape parameter and the inflection point



The number of breeding pairs in a colony of seabirds follows a Richards function with \(a=200\) pairs, \(b=0.3\)/year, \(c=10\) years and \(d=2\). How large is the colony when it grows fastest, as a number of pairs and as a fraction of its final size? How fast does it grow then? Compare the fraction with that of a logistic function.






TipSolution





The colony grows fastest at the inflection point, \(x=c=10\) years. Its size is then \(a\,(1+d)^{-1/d}=200\times3^{-1/2}\approx115\) pairs, a fraction \(3^{-1/2}\approx0.58\) of its final size, and it grows by \(ab\,(1+d)^{-1/d-1}=200\times0.3\times3^{-3/2}\approx11.5\) pairs/year. A logistic function (\(d=1\)) is steepest at half of its asymptote, so with \(d=2\) the fastest growth comes later in the approach to the asymptote.

title: Chapter 5: Deterministic functions in ecology — solutions
text:
1.1 Solution

1.1.1 Question 1
At \(x=0\) the function is \(f(0)=480/12=40\) mg, the mass of a seedling that grows alone. As \(x\to\infty\) the numerator stays at 480 while the denominator grows without bound, so \(f(x)\to0\): the function is a hyperbolic decline from \(a/b\) to zero. The parameter \(b=12\) is added to \(x\), so it is a number of seedlings per pot, and \(a=480\) has the units of \(y\) times those of \(x\) (mg times seedlings per pot).
Close to zero, where \(x\ll12\), the denominator is almost 12 and the function stays close to 40 mg. Far from zero, where \(x\gg12\), the denominator is almost \(x\) and \(f(x)\approx480/x\), so the mass of a seedling is inversely proportional to the number of seedlings. Between the two, at \(x=12\), the function has halved, \(f(12)=480/24=20\) mg. A sketch therefore starts at 40, passes through 20 at \(x=12\) and flattens towards zero.


1.1.2 Question 2
At \(x=0\) we have \(e^{0}=1\), so \(f(0)=90\,(1-1)=0\). As \(x\to\infty\) the exponential \(e^{-0.2x}\) goes to zero and \(f(x)\to90\) kg/ha, which is the amount of nitrogen that the residue can release. So \(a=90\) has the units of \(y\), and \(b=0.2\) multiplies \(x\) inside an exponential, so it is a rate, with units 1/week.
For a small argument the exponential is close to its tangent line at zero, \(e^{-u}\approx1-u\). With \(u=0.2x\),
\[
f(x)\approx90\,\bigl(1-(1-0.2x)\bigr)=90\times0.2\,x=18\,x,
\]
so close to zero the function is a straight line through the origin with a slope of \(ab=18\) kg/ha/week. The sketch starts along that line and bends towards the horizontal line at 90.


1.1.3 Question 3
At \(x=0\) the numerator is zero, so \(f(0)=0\). For the limit we divide the numerator and the denominator by the highest power, \(x^2\):
\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{30x^2}{100+x^2}
=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{30}{100/x^2+1}=30.
\]
So the function saturates at \(a=30\) seeds/night. Close to zero, where \(x^2\ll100\), the denominator is almost 100 and \(f(x)\approx30x^2/100=0.3\,x^2\). This is a parabola, which has a slope of zero at the origin and becomes steeper as \(x\) increases. The Michaelis–Menten function starts as a straight line, \((a/b)\,x\). That is the difference between the two functions: the Holling type III function starts flat, accelerates and then saturates, so it is sigmoid. The rodents remove almost no seeds when seeds are scarce. Note that the formula contains \(b^2=100\), so \(b=10\) seeds/m², and \(f(10)=30\times100/200=15\), half of the asymptote.


1.1.4 Question 4
The domain starts at \(x=5\) mg, where the fraction is zero and \(f(5)=2\) eggs. As \(x\to\infty\) the fraction is a Michaelis–Menten function of \(x-5\) and goes to 10, so \(f(x)\to2+10=12\) eggs. In the notation of the theory, the function is shifted by \(c=5\) mg along the \(x\) axis and by \(d=2\) eggs along the \(y\) axis, with \(a=10\) eggs and \(b=15\) mg.
Close to the lower end, where \(x-5\ll15\), the denominator is almost 15 and
\[
f(x)\approx2+\frac{10}{15}\,(x-5),
\]
a straight line that starts at the point (5, 2) with a slope of \(a/b\approx0.67\) eggs/mg. The function is halfway between 2 and 12, at 7 eggs, when \(x-5=b\), that is, at \(x=20\) mg. So the sketch starts at (5, 2), passes through (20, 7) and levels off below 12.


1.1.5 Question 5
At \(x=0\) the function is zero. As \(x\to\infty\) the factor \(x^2\) grows and \(e^{-0.4x}\) decays. The exponential dominates any power, so the limit is zero. With L’Hôpital’s rule, applied twice because the first application still gives \(\infty/\infty\):
\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{0.5\,x^2}{e^{0.4x}}
=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x}{0.4\,e^{0.4x}}
=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{0.16\,e^{0.4x}}=0.
\]
Close to zero the exponential is almost one, so \(f(x)\approx0.5\,x^2\): the function starts as a parabola, with a slope of zero. A Ricker function starts as the straight line \(ax\), with a slope of \(a\). So both functions are humps that start and end at zero, but this one rises slowly at first and then accelerates, which the Ricker function cannot do. Since the function is zero at both ends and positive in between, it must have a maximum. The product rule gives \(f'(x)=0.5\,x\,(2-0.4x)\,e^{-0.4x}\), which is zero at \(x=2/0.4=5\).
We can verify our math with R by evaluating each function at the lower end of its domain, close to it and at a very large value of \(x\):

# The five functions of the exercise.
seedling_mass = function(x) 480 / (12 + x)
nitrogen = function(x) 90 * (1 - exp(-0.2 * x))
seeds_removed = function(x) 30 * x^2 / (100 + x^2)
clutch = function(x) 2 + 10 * (x - 5) / (15 + (x - 5))
power_exponential = function(x) 0.5 * x^2 * exp(-0.4 * x)

# Value at the lower end of the domain, close to it, and at a very large x.
seedling_mass(c(0, 0.5, 100000))

[1] 40.000000000 38.400000000  0.004799424

nitrogen(c(0, 0.5, 100000))

[1]  0.000000  8.564632 90.000000

seeds_removed(c(0, 0.5, 100000))

[1]  0.00000000  0.07481297 29.99999970

clutch(c(5, 5.5, 100000))

[1]  2.000000  2.322581 11.998500

power_exponential(c(0, 0.5, 100000))

[1] 0.0000000 0.1023413 0.0000000

# The approximations close to the lower end, at the same second value.
18 * 0.5

[1] 9

0.3 * 0.5^2

[1] 0.075

2 + 10 / 15 * (5.5 - 5)

[1] 2.333333

0.5 * 0.5^2

[1] 0.125

# A quick look at one of the functions; the others are drawn in the same way.
curve(seeds_removed(x), from = 0, to = 60,
      xlab = "Density of seeds (seeds/m²)", ylab = "Seeds removed (seeds/night)")








The values at the ends agree with the limits, and half a unit away from the lower end the approximations are close to the functions (for example, 9 against 8.56 kg/ha for the nitrogen). Figure 1 shows the five functions.
